utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. We're sitting with just three Judges today pursuant to Rule 15 bis, Judge Kwon being away on authorised Tribunal business. As matters stand, Dr. Karadzic, you have 45 minutes left for your cross-examination. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Ms. Mulaosmanovic.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the very outset, I would like to tell you that I have full compassion for what you went through on that day, and in terms of everything we all went through during the war. I'm not challenging what had actually happened. I'm just trying to shed more light on who might have done this. I hope that you were also thinking of those 50.000 or 60.000 Serbs when you said that it was hard during the war. It was hard for them, too, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what 50.000 or 60.000 you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, those who were under Muslim control. Well, that leads us to my next question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that's an improper line of questioning for this witness, as you well know. Stick to the topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency, but I really am interested. I would like to know whether Ms. Mulaosmanovic believes that it was hard for them in Sarajevo, just like for Serbs in Grbavica and other parts of Sarajevo. That is important, because that is part of her statement here; namely, that it was hard during the war, which I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was hard for everybody in Sarajevo. People did not look different, in terms of their ethnic backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if somebody wanted to kill someone, they couldn't know who it was that they were killing at a distance; right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I please ask for D202. It has been MFI'd, D202.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mulaosmanovic, while we're waiting for this, do you know where the Elektroprivreda building is?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I said that this building is on the same route, just a bit further away from the place where the tram was stopped?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One tram stop away or perhaps even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think it's one.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit more than one, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can establish that on the map. Is that where the School of Economics is as well?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a bit closer than Elektroprivreda.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Pero Kosoric, Bristol, the Social Welfare building, the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, is all of that nearby, and all of it is on the right-hand side, except for the tobacco factory, which is on the left?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's relatively close, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The tobacco factory is on the right and all the rest is on the left; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're facing Ilidza, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I meant, in terms of the direction that you were moving in. Now I'm going to read something out in English. It's a regular combat report. It's brief. It is dated the 19th of July, 1992. However, that was the situation as it was throughout the war. The same party held these positions throughout: [In English] "1. During the day, the enemy intensified its snipers activities, especially from the following directions: Pero Kosoric Square, Bristol --" [Interpretation] Bristol is a hotel; right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English]"... Elektroprivreda company, Socijalno, School of Mechanical Engineering, tobacco factory, Assembly, and Vrbanja Bridge."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Can you stop there, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to note a recurrence of something that's been raised before, and that is the inappropriate nature of embedding in a question related to a particular document a commentary or purported evidence that comes from the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tieger, that's not going over the heads of the Judges at all. We see it, but, of course, both you and, indeed, Dr. Karadzic know that we take no notice of it because it's not evidence in the case. But what it does do is to waste time. Dr. Karadzic, please refrain from making statements. That's all they are; they're not evidence. Questions can provide evidence which is the answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I just wanted to be very specific on this, that Bristol is a hotel. But I can read the whole document again, if you wish: [In English] "Mortar fire over the area of defence of 2nd Infantry Brigade around Vrbanja Bridge and Grbavica II is intensified. Grouping of enemy forces is noticed in the areas from where snipers were firing. They fired with rifle grenades and from infantry weapons from directions of Sirokaca towards Bosut Barracks."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Ms. Mulaosmanovic, that these facilities and these zones around the railroad were held throughout the war by the Serbs to the left of the Miljacka River and, on the right, the Muslim Army, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was the situation all the way up to the Dayton Accords?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where the positions were. The territories were divided this way, but this is 1992, July, when the tram was not operating at all. We are talking about 1995, when there was some kind of a cease-fire, when the tram was operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, now we are going to present a document from the time that you are talk the about. But we wish to establish that there weren't any territorial changes; namely, that these buildings were in the hands of either one side or the other side. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm telling you I don't know exactly where the positions were, but approximately that is how the territory was divided.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This has already been admitted, for identification, that is, so now we're going to move on. Can I now ask for the participants to cast a glance at -- actually, does the witness have this? Could the lady please be given a copy of these two bulletins of the news agency, and could a copy be placed on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. In relation to this previous document, Sirokaca, Bosut Barracks, I don't know about those places. I was talking about Pofalici, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's why I didn't want to ask you about that, because Sirokaca is further away, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 27th, please, the first document, the 27th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out in English, and you will receive an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If it's all set, then I can start. The first piece of news in this daily piece of news is: [In English] "Sarajevo. "From Vrbanja Most, seriously wounded pensioner, Malisa Bogdanovic in the Serb Sarajevo community of Grbavica. This is one of the more flagrant violations of agreement on the complete cessation of hostilities. Ten days ago, Muslim snipers positioned in the Mount Igman zone, supposedly under UN control, killed two civilians in the Serb community of Vojkovici." [Interpretation] Vojkovici is far away, but we have seen where Vrbanja Bridge is. The name of Malisa Bogdanovic is referred to here, and he was hit by a snipper on that same day when you were. So you do accept that on that day, there was an exchange of fire in that zone?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot testify on the basis of this. I only testify about where I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what calibre the weapon was that hit you?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No one ever told you that?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now have the other document placed on the ELMO, dated the 29th of February, 1995, the second piece of news. It says: [In English] "Sarajevo. Muslim fighters directed fire at the Lukavica Slavisa Vajner-Cita Military Barracks and the Serb communities of Grbavica, Vogosca, and the Kasindolska Street. There were no casualties among Serb soldiers or civilians. On the wider Sarajevo war-zone, Muslims continued their engineering works."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mulaosmanovic, can you see that combat activity, especially sniper activity in that zone, was practically an ongoing, everyday thing?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that, but I would like us to look at this together and to see whether this was an isolated incident or whether your tram got caught up in crossfire.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear any combat during the day. I took the tram to go into town, so I was walking from the tram stop to the College of Dentistry and back, and really I did not hear any gun-fire on that day, except for what happened on the tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, you were walking along Vuka Karadzica Street. That's what it was called. Actually, you took the tram by the cathedral; right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by the cathedral, but I don't remember walking along Vuka Karadzica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you do agree that that is four or five -- or, rather, three or four kilometres away from the Marsal Tito Barracks; right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Will the Prosecution be angry over the fact that we had not notified them of these "Srna" News before? Can we have this admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are not angry about getting it this morning, because they're small items. But the witness has not really dealt with it. She knows nothing about the things that were put to her. As these are newspaper articles, the reliability is questionable. Therefore, we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I assume that's just healthy cynicism, this journalism, rather than these documents in particular, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: But you're right, the witness didn't attest to them in any way at all. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, they won't be admitted. Dr. Karadzic, if you want to produce, as it were, corroborating evidence of these matters in a more formal way, of course, you're welcome to do so. But these reports are not in any way attested to by the witness, and so the veracity cannot be established.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the sake of fuller information, may I say that I fully agree in relation to the media; however, not in respect of correspondence from the ground, because they report on what they hear and what they see, and they are not involved in politics. However, at their headquarters, that's where people engaged in politics. That's a different story, and we'll be dealing with that. I would like to call up 65 ter 15524. Excellency, that is what you had asked for, that this be corroborated in a more formal way. 65 ter 15524.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I see the document, Dr. Karadzic, but, again, it's very unlikely that this witness is going to have any knowledge of the document or any knowledge of the matters to which it appears to pertain. So, again, I don't see that this witness is the proper conduit for the admission of this as evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position is that this is an official report of the 27th of February, 1995, about the events at that point of time in that sector. The president of the republic is being informed by the chief of staff, speaking about the events. Since this is a public trial, because I would like for our neighbours, Muslims, to know that the Serbs did not do everything that is being ascribed to them, this is evidence of what was happening precisely in the places where Ms. Mulaosmanovic was and passed through. This is the reason. In any case, this can be admitted as a document to confirm the theory of the Defence that this was not an act of deliberate criminal firing at the tram, but that this was a place where there was crossfire, and that Ms. Mulaosmanovic just happened to be in the middle of that crossfire. If I may continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, that is a matter you can raise as a general proposition in due course, but I'm concerned with what this witness can attest to. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, any observations?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Actually, when you look at the document on the second page, at paragraph 3, there is a reference to sniper fire in the Vrbanja Bridge sector, and that is, indeed, an issue here, and it was an issue in the General Milosevic case, and documents have been admitted in relation to the sniper fire in that area. So it has a certain relevance for this case. And other than the two newspaper articles, which are coming from a newspaper that is emanating -- disseminating propaganda, that was my concern about this newspaper. This is now an official document, and we wouldn't really have a problem with this to be admitted as it is, at least related to what this particular evidence is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that may be the case, but can this witness deal with it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness has already said she doesn't know about this, that's correct, yes. Perhaps it is a better way to put this in a Bar table motion. I only wanted to be fair, because one of the documents that are related to -- that are admitted in the associated documents deal with sniper fire in that area as well. That's why I wanted just to mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, that's very fair. But, of course, what I have on my screen doesn't deal with that. But are you saying as far as this document is concerned, you're happy for that passage that deals with sniper fire to be admitted in any event?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, there you are, Dr. Karadzic. So you can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D625.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With all due respect, I need to make a small correction. Namely, it is correctly noticed by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff that paragraph 3 confirms the news agency report, but for the sake of clarity I would like to say that "Srna" is not a newspaper, it's a state news agency, so the reporter from the ground has no idea about what he's supposed to be reporting on. So it's not a matter of propaganda, but just factual reporting from the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it's now been admitted, so you have your point, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 65 ter 14715.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have a statement directed -- we were directed to by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff yesterday. This is your statement, Ms. Mulaosmanovic -- actually, Ms. Cehajic before. This is a statement given to Goran Kulenovic, as you can see this talks about the incident on the 27th of February, 1995: "I was returning home by tram from the city, where I had to go for health-care services at the Dental Clinic." And then do you know that units of the B and H Army were stationed in the Dental Clinic and at the Faculty of Dentistry?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that the clinic and the Faculty of Dentistry are opposite from the Medical Faculty in Kosevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have documents that speak to that. That unit was stationed there throughout the whole period. Do you know that the place where Nemanja and Mose Pijade Streets intersect? I know the old names of the streets, so between the Medical and the Dental Faculty there was a base with barricades, a base of the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, thank you. Because you had to have come from somewhere, because you would have seen that. This was on the street. Can we admit this, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't really see a purpose to admit the statement, but of course we don't have any objections against it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I didn't think you would. Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D626, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 09733. This is a 65 ter number. 09733.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This has been admitted as Exhibit P435, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I have the Serbian version here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report of the United Nations, Bosnia and Herzegovina Command. It's a report on the situation of the 27th of February, 1995. And then we have item 2, where it says: "Sector Sarajevo. "The level of armed incidents has reduced, but it's still above normal for this sector. The sector is close to the airport and Holiday Inn, where most active three CFVs were recorded." This is probably some kind of abbreviation about an incident. And then the paragraph third from the top in section 2 says: "A 44-millimetre mine, probably originating from the B and H, allegedly fired from the territory under B and H-controlled territory, fired yesterday in Eastern Dobrinja. There were no victims." Can we please look at the next page in the English. The last paragraph in that page, it says: "A tram was fired on that was moving between these two items, the results of which is one confirmed civilian victim and perhaps another three."

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Confirmed victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is page 9 in the English: "The victim sustained leg injury. It is estimated that the fire originated from DD907589. The trams stopped operating after this incident. Both parties participated in an armed conflict 300 metres farther at that time, in the Vrbanja Bridge sector. Both sides in this case were ascribed to -- were allegedly guilty of committing cease-fire violations by firing from machine-guns." And then the rest of this referred to Igman. It says here in the next paragraph: "At 950 hours, a number of bursts were fired at an aircraft while at low altitude ...," and so on and so forth. Do you believe that this report by the United Nations speaks about an exchange of fire or a crossfire into which your tram drove into and that these bursts of fire were not the results of sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if you place a sight on a different type of rifle would constitute a sniper rifle. An expert would need to talk about that. I don't know. The Vrbanja Bridge is far enough from the buildings, physically, so as the tram was passing I didn't hear any fire at all. So I think this is talking about a completely different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We saw that on the map. But tell us, Ms. Mulaosmanovic, is that in your statement that first you heard shots, and then after that bullets started hitting the tram, and you concluded that this was not B and H Army fire because the shots were not that close?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They couldn't be heard that loudly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you could hear them before they actually hit the tram. The first burst of fire did not hit the tram?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the impact, so I don't know if this was something that was perhaps heard at the front of the tram.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In order to be specific and to confirm what happened at the Clinic of Dentistry, can we look at 1D421. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I went to have an X-ray of my tooth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is why, Ms. Mulaosmanovic, I said right at the beginning that I'm not disputing what actually happened to you. All I want is that for you, the participants, as well as the public, to know that this is was not --

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just went in in the most ordinary way. I didn't notice anything unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a bulletin --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would just like to hear what the relevance of this document is. It is actually from the 29th of May, 1993, and therefore I wonder what the relevance is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic, what is the relevance? I was going to wait until I'd seen the contents first, but if you can assist us at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to show that Ms. Mulaosmanovic was moving among purely military objects, rather legitimate targets. And on the following page, will you see from their sources, from Muslim sources, sources of the Muslim Army, what was located at the Dental Clinic and the Faculty of Dentistry. This has already been admitted. I would like us just to see that each sector was dangerous, not because there was indiscriminate fire, but because everything was full of legitimate targets. Can we look at the following page. Just one look and then we will finish with it, because this is a document that has already been admitted. This is 1D, not D421.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mulaosmanovic, this is a bulletin of the B and H Army: "Insufficient responsibility in maintaining the secrecy of military data on combat readiness, use and intention of units, is noted among members of the Independent Battalion under the command of Adnan Solakovic, which is located in the premises of the Dental Technical School, the Faculty of Dentistry, Sarajevo." I don't know if you knew this or not. But now you can see from Muslim sources that a unit was located there and that that faculty was a legitimate target, and God forbid you could have been exposed to fire there.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go there in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this was until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I understand this document has already been -- has not been admitted, but at the moment I don't see the relevance of it. It's two years' difference in time between the incident that this witness is attesting to and the suggestion that the dental unit had a military presence. And she wasn't shot at the dental unit; she was shot at a tram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, I can see no conceivable basis how this can be admitted through this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the intervention is fine. But this was in 1992 and 1993 and 1995. This was a permanent base of this Independent Battalion unit at the Faculty of Dentistry. So all over Sarajevo, there could have been legitimate fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also just want to mention that the Prosecution objects to the admittance of that document with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I neglected to ask you, but I assumed that you would. You have eight minutes left, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 65 ter 90120, page 43. For your information, this is a transcript -- actually, this is document P484, the transcript of the 7th of October, 2008. And in the transcript, the driver confirms seeing soldiers in the tram. Can we look at the following page, page 45, please. 45, two pages on, where it says Witness MP-229, in the middle of this paragraph, he says: "Around 12.15 on 27 February ..." [In English] "... 1995, the witness was driving a crowded tram westward along Smaja od Bosne from the center of Sarajevo to Ilidza. There was a cease-fire in place at the time, and there had been no combat activities near or around the tram ..." [Interpretation] And then, on page 55, the answer in line 19: [In English] "No. What I said was that the soldier was standing next to me, and we started chatting as I was driving, and it turned out that we had been colleagues ...," and so on. [Interpretation] Next question: [In English] "In any case, we have the statements on record." [Interpretation] And so on and so forth. And then page 56: [In English] "... because he was a soldier because he was wearing an Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina uniform, but how would I know." [Interpretation] So let us have a full picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were uniform persons on the tram; right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me? I told you yesterday. The driver is in the front part, I was in the back part. I did not see. Even if there was a soldier in there, I see no reason to target a large number of civilians who were there in addition to the soldier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is a Prosecution exhibit, although we don't mind offering it ourselves. Now, from this same binder we'd like to have Map number 12, April 2009. The page number is 0546-6580. The 65 ter number is 1355 -- 13578, rather. 13578 is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mulaosmanovic, do you recognise this city map of the part of town where you lived?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark your street for us? You will find Marko Marulic here, Fojnicka, Sakiba Nisica.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it. I think it's here [marks], this street here, yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see. That is a particular concentration, but the street goes all the way to the railway?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it doesn't go on. It ends there. That's where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The street is Branka Blazek, right, and it intersects with two other streets; right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It actually goes to a particular building, and I don't know whether it continues after that building. I don't know whether it continues or not. I mean, I see it here as it is marked here. It's a sort of building, the yellow area here, and I don't know whether it continues beyond the railroad. It's an area where there are houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put a circle around the Pofalici neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is part of the Pofalici neighbourhood. It goes further down towards the School of Economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the hilly part up here? That's the Serb part of the neighbourhood, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you mark where your house is and place the number 1 by it. Maybe you still live there.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the dot, and this is number 1 [marks]. I hope you can see it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any military installations there at Drinska, on the railroad, then the railways station is nearby? Were there any military installations or military objectives there? Paromlinska as well. Units, positions?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, administrative services of the army were somewhere around there, but there were no positions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you not tell us that a sniper bullet landed in your building?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it came from a sniper, but a bullet did fly in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you think that it had to be a Serb bullet; rather, fired from the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is a trace on the wall. I looked through this hole in the window that the bullet had come through, and I saw that Vraca, the monument, could be seen up there. I cannot say anything for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you think is the distance between Vraca and your apartment?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, I don't know. But I know that these buildings where we lived were also hit by anti-aircraft bullets and anti-aircraft guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you told us that it was a bullet from a rifle that hit your house?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I think it came from a rifle. I'm not very knowledgeable about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at the ratio down here, the scale. One kilometre is twelve centimetres. Can you see that? Vrace is 18 centimetres away from your building, that is to say, a kilometre and a half. Do you allow for the possibility that it was someone else who was closer to you that had actually fired, because the Serb front-line is at least a kilometre and a half away from your apartment; as the crow flies, that is?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a bullet does fly as the crow flies. I'm not sure. I told you that I peered through this opening in the wall, and you can see the monument at Vrace there. I'm not very knowledgeable about what kind of weapons can be used. Also, death-sowers had quite a range, so I don't know what the distance could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, certainly less than a rifle.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I told you already I am not very knowledgeable about this. You have to ask someone who was more of an expert, but -- it's someone who knows more about this who should speak about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you put a circle around Vrace?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over here, it says "Vraca" [marks]. Now, I'm not sure whether the monument is to the left of the lettering, but I did see the monument through my window. Here, it says "Vraca." That is what's written here, if I'm not mistaken, it's in this red circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid it's in the part to the south-east to the place that you marked.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly it's not -- it's possible.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear Dr. Karadzic at all, overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you place number 2? Number 2 is by the park and number 1 is your apartment.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Ms. Mulaosmanovic, that Hrasno and this area between this monument and your apartment includes many tall buildings, apartment buildings?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but somehow from my window they couldn't be seen at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you put the date there, and can you put your initials on this city map?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 15th, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 15th of September.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Last question, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit D627.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ms. Mulaosmanovic, last question. Would you really be angry if somebody were deceiving you and if someone had ascribed to the Serbs something that had been done to you? Would that be very bad for the purposes of reconciliation there?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that were to happen, I would be angry, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wish you a safe trip.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just one question, Ms. Mulaosmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I state the obvious for the written record. You're wearing a head-scarf today. Can you recall whether or not you were wearing a head-scarf on the day that you were shot?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I have been wearing one since 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the conclusion of your testimony. Thank you very much for assisting the Court, and you're now free to go, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Have a safe journey home.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm also now leaving because someone else takes over; in fact, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your assistance, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: The next witness is Major Thomas, and we're ready when the Court is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Let him be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Can you state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Francis Roy Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Major Thomas, let me first address some preliminary formalities associated with the submission of your written evidence. Did you meet with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor in May last year and prepare a statement amalgamating the evidence you have previously given in this Tribunal, which you then signed on the 13th of May, 2009?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review that statement?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I believe that there are some corrections you would like to make to that statement. Mr. Registrar, can we please have 22966, please. Looking at the document on the screen in front of you, do you confirm that this is a list of corrections you wish to make to the statement, and that that is your signature at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that. And, yes, that is my signature at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Now, with those clarifications and corrections, can you confirm that the statement is accurate, and that if you were asked the same questions on the same topics today, your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in those circumstances, I tender 65 ter 22287 in conjunction with the document currently on the screen, which forms Major Thomas' 92 ter statement. I'd also note, Your Honour, that as indicated in our final Rule 92 ter notification, the Prosecution does not intend to tender all parts of this statement, nor the exhibits associated with certain parts. So a redacted version of the statement has been up-loaded, and that is now tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement which is 65 ter 22287 will be Exhibit P1558. And the clarification and correction to the statement will be Exhibit P1559.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I'll now read a brief summary of the evidence in Mr. Thomas' -- Major Thomas' statement. Major Roy Thomas was the senior military observer in Sarajevo from 14 October 1993 until the 14th of July, 1994. Major Thomas has 35 years of military experience with the Canadian Armed Forces. And prior to his arrival in Sarajevo, he had participated in five UN peacekeeping or military observer tours. Major Thomas authenticates a series of UNMO daily situation reports which show that in the months leading up to the Markale Market incident in February 1994, shelling activity in Sarajevo was intense. According to these situation reports, Bosnian Serbs frequently appeared to randomly shell the city and fire not only in areas around the confrontation line, but also into residential areas. The reports also tally the outgoing and incoming fire into Sarajevo on those days. In the week of 19 to 26 December 1993, for example, 6.565 projectiles were observed fired into Sarajevo, compared to 709 into the area controlled by the SRK. The issue of ongoing artillery fire into the city was raised with the Bosnian Serb Army, Sarajevo Romanija Corps headquarters at Lukavica Barracks, by both UNMO Sarajevo and UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo. Major Thomas observed that after the shelling incident at Markale Market, a cease-fire was quickly implemented under the threat of NATO air-strikes, and shelling activity in Sarajevo effectively stopped, as reflected in UNMO observations and the number of daily casualties caused by shelling. However, in the months that followed, civilian casualties caused by Bosnian Serb sniping increased, as indicated by UNMO records for the periods March to June 1994. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Major Thomas, UNMO reports during the period you were in Sarajevo describes shelling into residential areas. Did you personally observe shelling into residential areas?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And from observing this shelling, were you able to determine its purpose?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I could see no military value in anything that was being shelled in those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And why did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: There was no military target that they could be attacking with shells. It just seems to be -- seemed to be random into buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: What type of shelling would you have expected to see if the attacker was intent on neutralising or destroying a specific target or specific targets?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, I would have expected, from my experience as a combat arms officer, that they would have acquired a target, identified it as a military target which would affect -- or military objectives, they would engage it, and then they would observe the effects of their fire on that military target and adjust their fire and try and neutralise or destroy the target. If there's nothing visible, there's very little -- I mean, it's the normal practice for using military artillery fire to support a military objective, wasn't -- couldn't apply in this situation, and there was no apparent target analysis of what they'd hit. And they were using the same vantage points that we were; high ground overlooking the city, and if they couldn't -- if we couldn't see what damage was being done, they couldn't either. So not only were they firing on a target that we couldn't identify as being military, but they couldn't even analyse what they had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Major Thomas, I'd like to clarify a few aspects of the UNMO daily situation reports. This is discussed at paragraphs 36 to 38 and 89 to 96 of your statement. Were you responsible for producing these reports?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I was responsible for the daily situation report which came from UNMO Headquarters Sarajevo, and I personally prepared the commander's assessment for UNMO Sarajevo situation reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I'd like to take a look at an example of one of those reports. Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 10575, please. This is a situation report for the 24-hour period from 6.00 p.m. on the 25th of December until 6.00 p.m. on the 26th of December, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Now, we see, in the first paragraph, under the head "General Assessment," and if we look to the -- beginning on the third line, it states: "The residential areas shelled today were ..." And then we see a list of places. And if we go down to the seventh line, we see it is written. "The areas considered close to the confrontation line were ..." And again a list of places. On what basis, Major Thomas, did you report that shelling had occurred in those areas?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: My military observers in the five observation posts and team sites within the city of Sarajevo or overlooking the city of Sarajevo would have observed this fire. They would have sent a consolidated report in time to reach my headquarters usually by 5.00, so that we could prepare this report which was sent at 6.00 local time to Zagreb and Sector Sarajevo. So this would be a compilation of reports sent in by my team sites in the city and sometimes by the team sites outside the city who observed shells falling on Sarajevo. And my operations staff would process this and then prepare this report. And usually if I had time, if I was just returning, I would get a briefing on where these shells had fallen on a map, because all these reports would also be plotted on a master map each day in my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Major Thomas, do you believe that the information reflected in these situation reports is an accurate reflection of the reality of the shelling in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: This is an accurate reflection of the shelling as observed by my observer teams. We did not get to see everything. We had only five OPs, and if you were looking in one direction or trying to get bearings on one impact area, you might miss some other impact somewhere else. Also, we were limited that we had no night capability, so at night we were basing our reports on the sounds of shells falling in an area, and perhaps the flashes if we were quick enough to see it. So we had no night capability to observe the fall of fire. Many of the shells fell into areas where it would be hard to observe their actual hitting on the ground, and we would be basing it on plumes of smoke or debris which arose from the fire. But this represents -- and I stand by the reports of my teams. This represents the shelling that was occurring as could be observed by the five team sites which were set up on purpose to observe the shelling of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement the term "UNMO confirmed." What did that mean?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: "UNMO confirmed" meant that we did, to the best our ability, within the restrictions that I've just listed -- that we saw and we reported what we saw. And there was always two people on the site of two different nationalities, and they had to agree on the total that was sent in. And somebody sometimes, perhaps a more experienced military observer, might feel that there had been more shots, more artillery fire, or less. Also, you must recognise that the countries sent observers, some of whom are air force or navy, and it is a skill to determine what type of shell is falling, when you have heavier calibre, like 152-millimetre, mixed in with 81-millimetre mortar. So when there's a large amount of shelling, then the smaller calibre of rounds, the impacts may be masked by the heavier rounds. And as an example, in the reports that are submitted as part of the evidence, you will note that my observers on one particular report noted that they counted 858 impacts, but, in fact, my observers on the Bosnian Serb side observed 1600 artillery rounds being fired, and this discrepancy is due to the fact we couldn't see where all the rounds fell. So if anything -- to say that it's an accurate reflection, I would say probably we understated the number of shells that were being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: During your tour, Major Thomas, did you have any reason to think that any of your military observers were biased in their reporting?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, and if I would have found a guy that was biased, he would have left the sector immediately. He would have been taken from his OP immediately and brought down to headquarters, and put on the next available plane. And I had military observers sent from Sector Sarajevo within 24 hours for doing things that I didn't think they were following the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If we turn back to the situation report on our screen, and looking at the general assessment again, why did you consider it important to draw a distinction between areas near the confrontation line and residential areas?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: This is based partly on the fact that Zagreb wanted us to make this distinction and partly on the fact that all of us, as military observers, were very closely following the actual combat along the confrontation line. So for most of us, where these shells were falling where there was no target or military value, we couldn't understand how it would have any influence on the battle at the confrontation line. I mean, we're watching the confrontation line, and obviously shells that are falling there could influence the conflict. But the ones that were falling at random in the city, as I have already stated, the military value of these rounds didn't make sense to any of us. And the distinction is important to see how much ammunition is being spent on firing at random into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Major Thomas, in another of your situation reports around the same time - for the record, this is the situation report for 26th to 27th December, which is 65 ter 10576 - you list the areas shelled on or near the confrontation lines, and then you remark in the report that: "Take note that these areas still contain civilians." Why did you make this note?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Because I was afraid the headquarters staff in Zagreb would lose track of the fact that lots of people in Sarajevo had to live on houses -- in houses on the confrontation line because they had no other accommodation. There was no refugee camp. They were in a city that was surrounded, and they couldn't get out. So given the choice of being close to the area where the confrontation line was and having no accommodation in the middle of winter, I think most of them said they'd take a chance to themselves. I never questioned them, but I assumed that that was the reason why. And people tended to forget, although it was a confrontation line, it was still the homes of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, the general assessment, we see the letters "GR," and then four-digit numbers. What do those represent?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, that's the grid square, and that is, again, designed to help the duty officer in Zagreb quickly pick up the area where this is happening and noting it. For example, if there was a grid square that was dealing with an area of the city, he'd look on the grid square and, for example -- and once that sitrep, probably we're talking about an area of the city and there would be some major arteries. And once that's highlighted, the duty officer in Zagreb can go and say, Well, the shells are falling along the road or in the area, and he would know it. Obviously, the shells wouldn't be falling on the whole grid square because there's some vacant areas in some of these, but it's an aid to get the guy in Zagreb zeroing in right on that area of the city where the shells are falling, and then he can go -- the usual pattern where people are moving.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can we have 65 ter 09390D, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Major Thomas, did you have the opportunity to discuss with the Prosecution, upon your arrival in The Hague, the way in which you might visually depict those grid references on a map?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And looking at the map in front of you, is that a correct depiction of the grid references from the situation report that was on our screen a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, and I can use my electronic pen to show how the duty officer would be -- had the grid squares marked. That's it there [indicates]. And then he would be able to track, when he's briefing somebody, the area where the shells are falling, the general area that we would -- so, in actual fact, in that case on that sitrep, I suspect that the road that people used behind the buildings to avoid going down sniper alley was being shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender into evidence the unmarked version of that map, in addition to the situation report that was on our screens a moment ago. I'd also note at this point that in light of Major Thomas' testimony about these grid references, it's the Prosecution's intention to submit an exhibit, by way of Bar table, of maps for each of the situation reports that will come in through Major Thomas to visually depict those grid references in the general assessment, as a way to assist the Chamber to understand what that information was conveying at the time. We intend to do that by way of written motion in the coming days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objection to the admission of the map and the document? No. So be it, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the unmarked map will be Exhibit P1560, and the sitrep, which is 65 ter number 10575, will be Exhibit P1561.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And while we're on the topic of situation reports, 65 ter 21991, please. That's the correct document. Just for the purposes of the transcript, it should read "21991."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Major Thomas, looking at this document, can you confirm that this is the UNMO Sarajevo situation report for the time-period 1800 hours until one minute before midnight on the 4th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, it says it's an update.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And if we turn to page 2, again, can you confirm that this was the update or situation report for the period one minute after midnight until 800 hours on the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I ask that to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1562, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: 65 ter 21694, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: At paragraph 74 of your statement, Major Thomas, you describe a sample list of weapons identified by the UN as possible targets in the case of air-strikes, and you refer to the document we're seeing on our screens now. Do you know who was responsible for creating or authoring this list?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: This list was authored or created by NATO, primarily based on aerial surveillance. I had no role in creating this list. My function was to send teams out to these sites to verify that this equipment was being moved, or in the process of being moved, or actually had already been moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Approximately what date did you send people out?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: We sent it as soon as this report was received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And do you -- sorry. And do you recall approximately when that was during your tour?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I couldn't say. What's the date on the -- the date we received this, I can't read the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If it assists: Was it before or after the Markale Market --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, this is after Markale. NATO didn't get involved at all before, and so it was after. And the threat from NATO was that if this equipment wasn't moved, they would bomb it. And the impulse for us to act quickly was to get there and make sure it was moved, or if it wasn't moved before the next aerial surveillance was done, we had to account for why it wasn't being moved. And I have one specific example to just enlighten Your Honour. We had a case of six guns that were stuck in the snow, and they couldn't physically move them. They were fairly significant artillery pieces, but we had to send a patrol in there, make sure that we could explain why these guns could not be moved because of the deep snow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. If this document can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, that can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1563, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And one final document, Major Thomas, 65 ter 10585. Again, this is a document discussed in your statement at page 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe to the Court the information contained in this document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: This is information relating to sniper, and it's for both sides. You'll see "BSA" for Bosnian Serb, and "BiH" for Bosnian. And it's the grid, and we were trying to calculate if there was areas where sniper activity was high or low, and the kind of casualties that were occurring in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Do you consider this list to be a comprehensive list of sniping victims in Sarajevo in these four months?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I consider it to be a comprehensive list of what military observers were involved in. We were often called in to investigate sniper activity in the battalion areas of interest. On the other hand, sometimes they didn't ask us, and we have no idea what sniper activity occurred in their area for which we were not invited to. But this was an attempt on our part, and it is as complete as we could make it on the investigations that we did into sniper activity. And I can certainly say we missed some, and particularly in the area of the French battalions in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Finally, we see the determination -- notation "C" or "S" for each of the victims, "S" standing for "Soldier," and "C" standing for "Civilian," according to the key. On what basis or on what criteria did you or your military observers give this designation to a victim?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, you can see initially that we -- I want to make sure that the male and female distinction was only started on the 20th of June, and I have that note on the bottom of that. But the basic premise we worked on was that all males, whether they had a uniform or not, were potential soldiers, and the reason, one of the background reason for this, for example, our interpreters, that were male, were treated with destain by both warring parties because they weren't doing their bit fighting, they were considered traitors. It didn't matter which side they were. So the -- however, the context, and this was left to the judgement of independent -- of each -- independent judgement of each military observer, if they found somebody killed, a man killed in a situation, either he was old -- too old or too young to be likely to be a soldier, or it was the middle of the afternoon and there was no military area nearby, then we treat him as a civilian. And by the same token, if we had found a female killed in a trench, we would have had to treat her as a soldier, and certainly there were female soldiers. But as a general rule, males, even whether they were in uniform or not in uniform, were considered a possible soldier. But we did -- there was a judgement call and the distinction was made. If it's an obvious non-military situation, well, we can't really tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Thomas. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just looking at this document, where the grid reference is placed, is that the reference for the spot where a body or an injured person was found or is it the reference from where it's thought the shot came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a reference of where the body was found. In fact, in some cases we have no way of determining, and, in fact, I'd be quite frank, in some cases we would have to say it would be very hard to determine which side of the line the shot was fire from. The line had several weird bends and twists. But we assumed -- we made assumptions, but we just listed on that, as you see, where we found the body and which side -- which belligerent party he could be identified with, and that's all we tried to capture in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And the difference between the six- and the four-figured grids is simply the question of accuracy of the grid reference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Before I forget, I'd like to admit this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, that can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1564, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And at this point, Your Honour, I tender the remaining documents from the 92 ter statement, bearing in mind that in our final notification we marked those documents we're not tendering into evidence, and that included those documents that are already evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. They will all be admitted in sequence. And that's the end of your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Major Thomas, we'd normally have a break at this time anyway. It's a few minutes early, but it doesn't seem any point in commencing cross-examination only to stop it within two or three minutes. So we'll take a break now for 30 minutes. I'm sure you've been told this before. Every witness is told it. When you're in the middle of giving your testimony, please don't discuss the testimony you have given or the testimony you may give with anybody. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Allow me, before that, to introduce my new assistant present in the courtroom pursuant to an approval by the Trial Chamber, and he is standing in for Marko Sladojevic. This is Mr. Aleksandar Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Welcome, Mr. Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, good day.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I remind you of a number of your statements that were useful to me in throwing some light on the situation in which you were present. In the case against General Galic, transcript of the 30th of May, 2002, on page 9265, as well as in the case of the Prosecutor against President Milosevic of the 12th of November, 2003, page 28878, you stated that at the time when you arrived in Sarajevo, there was firing at the town -- there was ongoing shelling into the city: [In English] "... shelling on Papa 3 coming from the Bosnian Serb side because the Bosnians had located mortars not too far from Papa 3 post." [Interpretation] Did you state that on these two occasions?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did state that the Serbs fired on Bosnian mortars that were positioned too close to Papa 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Am I correct if I say that this happened frequently and that UNPROFOR officers had to lodge protests and requests that the Muslim Army officers move their weaponry away from positions of the United Nations? This includes the PTT building as well as Papa positions.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: We had to tell the Bosnians on several occasions to move mortars away from the positions because they were too close to UN buildings or facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And their firing on Serb positions prompted a response from the Serbian side, and in that way endangered the United Nations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. No more so than driving down sniper alley and getting shot at by a Serb sniper when we weren't anywhere near a Bosnian, though, I might add.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Major, sir. Yes, we will come to that. Let me just remind you of one other of your statements of the 18th of November, 1997. On page 0055-2648, you stated and you established that Muslims, as you say, Bosnian soldiers masked as Serbs, fired at the UNPROFOR commander for Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. That was a well-documented incident, and you don't need my testimony to elaborate further on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also, in your statement of the 13th of May, 2009, on page 19 you said that Bosniaks, which we understand to be Muslims, began to use tank fire from the town, with the intention of drawing a response -- retaliatory fire from the Serbian side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. They knew that you would retaliate to anything that they fired. We couldn't understand why you retaliated, why you didn't just let us investigate their violation of the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For your information, and we will prove that, the order to our army was to retaliate only when lives were in danger; thus, when it was no longer possible to bear the fire. Major, sir, in your daily reports for the Sarajevo Sector of the 25th of October, 1993 - this is 65 ter 10582 - establish that Bosnian or Muslim soldiers attacked a UNMO car, a military observer of the UN's vehicle, and attempted to remove -- [In English] "... jackets and helmets. Jackets and helmets were returned the day after. However, the radios were not." [Interpretation] Thus, they did not only attempt, but they actually took for a whole day these helmets and flak-jackets and radios; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. And, again, this is a well-documented incident, and it mainly dealt with the French Battalion, and it was their problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in your statement of the 18th of November, 1997, on page 55 to 648 [as interpreted], and in your statement of the 13th of May, 2009, on page 19, you asserted and affirm that Muslim forces, or Bosnian forces as you refer to them, seized a number of United Nations vehicles and APCs, armoured transporters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, and I went later on to say that this was a rogue brigade commander who was subsequently disciplined by the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I'm sorry to intervene. I just happen to be noticing that almost every time the witness answers, he adds some other element, essentially, that helps assist the Prosecutor, but in general I was wondering if you could advise him, given the limited amount of time that Dr. Karadzic has, it would be better for all of us if you could just simply answer the question, and if the Prosecution feels that they need more information, they have the chance to do re-examination. But I think he's adding new elements that is going to make it very difficult for us to complete his examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Robinson, it might be said that that was an example of the pot calling the kettle black, as they say in English, but it does, of course, help if you can, in terms of time management, Major Thomas, simply to restrict your answer to the question. I understand the temptation to elaborate may be sometimes overwhelming, but I'm sure you understand the point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the testimony in the Galic case of the 3rd of June, 2002, on pages 9427 and 28, you said that a report was prepared, that five Muslim outgoing -- I'm going to read it in English: [In English] "... rounds were observed. Destination unconfirmed. No impact were recorded on the Bosnian Serb side, and it was -- it is possible, even if very unlikely, that one or several of those five shots never arrived outside the premises of the town. There were rumours that the Bosnians would shell their own people." [Interpretation] Is it correct that this is what you stated in the Galic case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I'd have to see that again, because if we didn't see it -- observe the fall of shot, we could only make an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that there were rumours that Muslims were firing at their own people?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Rumours were never UNMO confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, sir, did UN Military Observers conduct thorough criminal legal investigations into these rumours about these incidents? Did they make proper inquiries?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It was not our mandate to conduct criminal legal investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then your reports were of an informative nature, they were information reports?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Our reports, as I've stated in my statement previously delivered to this Court, were to record the fall of shot that we observed, and to record the rounds fired by the Serb artillery that we were located close to, and also to record, if we saw it, rounds falling on the Serb side, and also to report, if we saw it or heard it, rounds being fired from the Bosnian side. Our mandate was not to conduct investigations unless requested by Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it would happen that some shells would be lost, like you said, on that occasion, and we saw in other documents as well that there is a discrepancy between fired shells and the shells that actually hit the other side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I've already stated this morning that we counted 858 impacts on the Bosnian side, and we had physically counted 1600 rounds being fired on the Serb side. Yes, in both sides of the line there were discrepancies between what was fired and what we observed to fall. We weren't in a position to do everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will probably come back to this. Major, sir, also in the Galic case, on the 3rd of June, 2002, on pages 9433 and 94434 [as interpreted], you said that these rumours about them killing their own people came about due to criminal activities or for political reasons, and you said, in particular, this referred to the need to increase the number of casualties and attract the sympathy and solidarity of the media; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd have to see again that document. I can't -- I would -- I could make a suggestion, but I would not assert it -- I would not say that a rumour was UNMO confirmed. It would be unconfirmed hearsay, in my opinion. And I might have been asked a view -- my view in that court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Just to note, I think we saw an example there of paraphrasing that is not helpful to the witness. Dr. Karadzic has helpfully taken us to the pages, but I think it's better if he quotes directly from the passages rather than paraphrasing the witness's prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes, it makes it easier. But we've now heard the question in this particular instance and we've heard the answer, so perhaps we can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can quote each one, but then we need more time. This answer was: "There were rumours that people were killed ..." [In English] "... on their own side for other reasons. "Q. Would those be political reasons, sir? "A. In some cases, it was suspected. In other cases, criminal activities." [Interpretation] Then there's a part that's skipped: [In English] "When you spoke, political reasons would be perhaps to -- media or was it perhaps to increase the figures for political reasons? "A. Certainly, there would be a political reason to do this. "Q. That is at the same time there would be more victims increasing, the number of victims, and also attracting the compassion of the media; is that how I am to understand your answer? "A. That would be true, although you will see, on the 9th of March, most casualties were Bosnian Serb Army." [Interpretation] This is the quote that we -- but we saw you confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall and do you now confirm this particular quote?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I -- at that time, I said there was a rumour. I didn't say it was fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we established that there were no inquiries conducted so that you would be able to establish that as a fact. The inquiries were not of a nature leading to a criminal or legal proceedings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then did you also, in the Galic case on the 3rd of June, on page P9435 [as interpreted], without being able to give the precise date, did you not say the following: [In English] "Did you know of at least one instance where there was a sniping incident which occurred for which there was no reason except that CNN was passing by within a certain time while the casualty would still be there?" And: "This occurred in June, but I can't be sure about that probably. "Q. Sir, thank you. Witness, for your relative precision of your answer, could you tell us if not when, then where did this happen? "A. This happened at a junction of the road from the airport and the road that leads into Dobrinja." [Interpretation] Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I made that statement, yes, and the only possible motive that appeared to us for killing an old man, over 65, would appear to be the passage of the CNN media crew. I stand by that statement. There was no -- that was the only reason. But we were never able to prove it, and we are not mandated to go further and investigate.
