Neither belligerent party, I might add, Your Honour, if you're interested in the background, neither belligerent party shared the location of their snipers with the military observers. It took a lot of hard work to get any disclosure about sniper locations from either side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you for that. The very nature, it may be said, of sniping is that the sniper is likely to fire and move. Otherwise, the sniper puts himself or herself at great risk. Yes, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope that you agree with the observation of His Excellency, Judge Morrison. Major, sir, are there cases when sniper activity is a completely legitimate military activity?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: When the target is military and there is justified military purpose to it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, sir, in the case against President Milosevic, on the 12th of November, 2003, on page 28885, and in your statement of the 13th of May, 2009, on page 21, did you not say the following? Let me just ask the Trial Chamber, should I continue with a brief interpretation or is it necessary for me to actually quote the entire passage? Would it be all right to summarise the passage, providing the exact page for the witness? Is it acceptable to proceed in this way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: If the summary is concise and accurate, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will do our best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that you took part in an investigation of an attack by Muslim soldiers on a Serb village near Han Pijesak, and that you noticed that Muslim forces burned to the ground each Serbian house in that area. You stated this in your statement of the 18th of November, 1997, on page 0055-2648. And in the case against President Milosevic, on the page that I previously quoted, you said that you had counted -- or that your count indicated that in that attack, all Serbs who were in the village were killed, regardless of gender and age; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, all right, thank you. Do you remember that village, and do you remember what happened? You remember that; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I remember that, and I stand by that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement of the 18th of November, 1997, on page 0055-2648, and in your statement of the 13th of May, 2009, on page 21, you stated that there was firing at a UN plane and that this episode was an attempt to induce the international community to intervene: [In English] "... intervene so as to fix the front-lines." [Interpretation] Do you remember this statement?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I'd have to get a closer look at that, because there is other incidents that I felt were more episodes trying to induce international community intervention, such as the killing of the six kids tobogganing and incidents like that. So firing at the planes may have been one of the incidents that I attribute, and that's public knowledge that I thought there were people trying to provoke the international community. And firing at a plane was a minor incident compared to the massacre of people in the market, the killing of people in the bread line, and the kids being killed on the toboggan hill. Your Honour, I can add to that, about the threat to the aeroplanes, and describe, for the edification of the Court, what action I took as a senior military observer, if you think it would assist in understanding this particular part of this little piece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. If you can do so concisely, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I deployed, from my limited resources, an observer team to the end of the runway. I instituted a number of patrols that covered the approach path to Sarajevo Airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The aircraft were targeted at low altitude, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were targeted as a -- they had to clear a high building that was on Serb territory and then come down and level off fairly quickly, and at that point they were considered quite vulnerable. So we were trying to make sure that small-arms fire, which had been encountered by aircraft at that point in time that Dr. Karadzic mentions, that they were not threatened if we could possibly deter people from firing. We also had patrols go out further looking for any anti-tank and anti-aircraft weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That may assist you, Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now pull up in e-court 65 ter 1 -- excuse me, it's 1D1615.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we are waiting: Major, sir, which of the warring sides in Bosnia and Herzegovina had an interest in causing an international intervention, international military intervention?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Are you asking for my judgement on this? Because I have no evidence to make a case for either side. Both -- I think there were people on both parties that would be interested in causing an international intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree, Major, sir, that all UN documents speak of the intentions and attempts by the Muslim forces to provoke a foreign military intervention, and that the Serbs did everything in order to prevent that because that intervention would be against their interests?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree that all UN documents said that. I'm not privy to the UN intelligence documents that might have suggested something different. And as you know, Dr. Karadzic, I wrote an article suggesting, in fact, there were people on the Serb side that would have wished the UN to intervene to fix the lines, and equally there were people on the Bosnian side who thought the attacks in Grbavica were succeeding quite well, any attacks on places like the village of Han Pijesak were succeeding very well, and that those things meant that eventually they could succeed without outside intervention. So there was a party on the Bosnian side that also felt they would get the military upper hand and their superior manpower would be winning out. So there are two parties on each side with those who want intervention and those that don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Just for the record, we've handed a translation of the document on the screen to the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand it doesn't exist in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Not as yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Major, sir. Since we have a translation now, could the witness please be given a copy. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So this is a regular combat report of 1700 hours for the 18th of October, 1993. The third paragraph -- the third subparagraph of paragraph 1 says: "While the UN aircraft -- while the UN NATO aircraft was flying across Igman, the enemy opened fire at it using a PAM, 12.8 millimetres, from the area of the village of Lokve, Paljanski Put, the Pale road." And it says here: "Our units responded and opened fire using infantry weapons." The deputy commander of the corps is reporting to his headquarters that Muslim forces from Igman were opening fire at an aircraft that was flying over. Do you agree that Igman was under the control of the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Not completely, not at all. There was a part that was controlled by the Serbs and there was a part that was, I considered, no-man's land.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then we will have to have a look at the map at one point and then establish who was where. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, I haven't seen the translation yet. I can't comment on that document, and I have no record of a UN aircraft being fired at flying over Mount Igman. But I can say that all UN aircraft were fired at by both sides when they flew at night because we couldn't track who was doing the shooting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. The document can be admitted, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D628. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, sir, you have the document before you now. Could you look at subparagraph 3 of the first paragraph. That is what we have been discussing so far. I would just like you to be satisfied.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, not having any aeroplanes under my control, I can't comment on that report. That would have been reported by the French Sector headquarters, if it was one of their aircraft, and by the air component in the Zagreb headquarters if it was a NATO aircraft. If it was a NATO aircraft, it would have been not even under UN control and we might not ever have heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm just saying that because in this statement you mentioned that UN aircraft were being fired at, and that the reason was an attempt to provoke an international military intervention. Major, when you testified against President Milosevic on the 12th of November - 28875 is the page reference - did you say: [In English] "The Bosnians conducted a major attack on Grbavica. They were wearing French-style helmets and French-style flak-jackets"?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. And I think you saw in the corrections that I gave to the Prosecutor to clarify that statement. You received that this morning. Yes, I most certainly did see that, and I didn't say they were wearing -- I said I saw a French -- correction, Bosnians wearing equipment that I first identified as French. And this statement has been handed out. I did not see them physically conducting an attack. I saw them crossing a road into an area from which assaults were originating. And as I clarified this morning, I said that at first glance, I thought they were French troops because of the equipment they were wearing, but on closer inspection and when I got closer, I could see that they were not French troops. And as I stated in my statement that was given to Your Honour this morning, I clarified that to make sure that people in this Court understood that I had no evidence that French equipment was given to the Bosnians. And I can go on to further elaborate. I felt that anything in Sarajevo was for sale and that people could obtain almost anything they wanted if they had money. Unfortunately for us poor soldiers, we didn't have enough money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Sir, I think a common complaint amongst soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, how close did you have to get in order to establish it wasn't the French?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I was 10 feet away from them. I could see the helmets were under camouflage or they were not blue-coloured. I got out and challenged them and asked -- and determined then at that time that they were Bosnian soldiers. You must remember this is at night. Because of the shelling of the city, the only people that had lights on were UN. Because of the close proximity to the front-line, I chose to drive without my lights on because I didn't want to expose any of the belligerents in the light of my vehicle lights. So I was driving black-out, and the people, of course, were crossing in complete darkness, and there was no street lighting. There was no street lighting in Sarajevo during my time there at night. The only lights on were in the UN compounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, but I'm waiting for the interpretation to finish. That's why I'm pausing. Then, Major, in your statement dated the 13th of May, 2009, on page 10, and in your statement dated the 18th of November, 1997, on page 0055-2648, you established that, as a matter of fact: [In English] "For the major part, it was unsuccessful, according to your opinion, this was a very well-co-ordinated attack which made a good use of Bosnian assets, infantry, artillery, and tanks." [Interpretation] That's in the first statement of the 13th of May, 2009. And then further on you say: [In English] "... demonstrated the Bosnian level of command and control ..." [Interpretation] That's in the other statement, dated the 18th of November, 1997; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, it isn't right. At no point would I have said that Bosnians had assets of artillery and tanks. I think you'd have to repeat the writing as I stated it. The Bosnian asset that they had was infantry. The Serbian asset, from my point of view as a military officer of 35 years, was artillery and tanks, and at no time did the Bosnians have an asset that I would call anything more than token of tanks and artillery. They had mortars, but as I would go on to say, they at no time during my time there used anything heavier than a 120-millimetre mortar. They had no field artillery of any kind that was used during my time there. So they did a very well-co-ordinated attack in Grbavica, and they attacked on several different axes, forcing your limited Serb resources to deploy facing attacks from three different points on the clock, and they were attacking at night with infantry in a built-up area, whereas your military advisers would tell you tanks and artillery are quite ineffective, particularly at night if they have no vision equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As the witness has noted, he has been misquoted in the transcript. At that paragraph, he, in fact, stated that: "It appeared to be a very well-co-ordinated attack, making good use of the Bosnian asset, infantry, to combat the Serb asset, artillery and tanks."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness has made that plain. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if this questioning persists where he misquotes what I have previously given in testimony under oath, I'd like him to read the statement, regardless of how long it takes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I can understand your concern, but I equally have no doubt, from what I've heard so far, of your ability to correct any misquotation. Dr. Karadzic, it doesn't help. It wastes an awful lot of time if we have to revisit and then revisit again passages because they've been inaccurately summarised. I said summaries are fine, but the motivating words are accuracy and con cision.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What happened here was, indeed, that the major meant Serb tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, Major, in the town of Sarajevo, itself, did the Muslims have tanks, Howitzers, mortars, 60, 82, and 120 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: They had some tanks and some heavy artillery which I never saw used. It was stored in a tunnel. In fact, we found one tank in a basement of a house which they couldn't have gotten out, as we couldn't get it out when it came time to collect it. So they brought out two tanks in June to provoke you into trying to retaliate and to demonstrate, perhaps, to people that thought they had no army, just infantry, that they did, in fact, own tanks. We were already aware of that, but they never brought them out of the tunnel. And I'm just surprised that with your artillery assets, you never blocked the tunnel so they would never be able to use it in a counter-attack. If you'd used some of the shells you shot into the village into blocking the tunnels so they wouldn't get this equipment out, in case you actually did do an attack, it would have been much better use of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that that tunnel was not in depth into the territory, it's not on the separation line, and it links Velesici and Ciglane? It goes underneath Kosevo Hill from Velesici towards Ciglane, and it's far away from the front-line. When firing at that tunnel, one does not fire at the separation line, but in depth into the territory?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: You seem to have no problem firing at depth into the territory in the case of what I consider random residential areas, so I'm surprised, as I just said in my previous statement, that if you're going to fire that far into the city to try and hit -- retaliate against mortars firing from the area of the hospital, that you would, in fact, fire at the tunnel. Rubble blocking the tunnel would have prevented any of that equipment from being used. You had the guns, by the way. The 152-millimetre had the range from some of its locations, and you also had the 122 artillery gun, and both of these have the ranges that could reach anywhere. And that's why the exclusion zone was 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Major, we are going to show you a document of yours now -- actually, a UN document that confirms that the Muslim side was firing at us from a residential area. You did admit that you could not establish all the circumstances involved all the time. Why are you saying that Serbs fired at residential areas for no reason whatsoever, while Serbs were actually being fired at from residential areas? Do you allow for the possibility that there were reasons at the time why there were -- there was fire opened at residential areas, but you were not aware of those reasons at the time?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: We were aware that the Bosnians tried to provoke you into firing. It was one of their favourite hobbies, might I say, to provoke Serb retaliatory fire. It would have been a much better use of resources if you followed the standard artillery practice of what we call counter-battery fire. Instead of firing at the last known location of the guns that fired at you, you fire at where you think they're going to move to. And we were never able to establish what you were firing at, because you, unfortunately, never did any target assessment. And any time we got to the area, we found there were no mortars in the area at all, so they had moved, not surprisingly, because of the way artillery often you fired in that direction would have blown the mortars away. But you gave them time to move to another location where we couldn't discover them. And rest assured, Dr. Karadzic, we did make efforts to try to catch Bosnians violating artillery protocols as well. I hate to say it, but for a professional army that I thought so many of the officers of the Bosnian Serb Army were, some of the Bosnian tactics proved to be superior, and one of them, I think, deserves some look by military analysts, not necessarily in this court, is how they managed to use the mortars and get them moved so quickly and avoid any semblance of counter-battery fire on your part. Instead of retaliating, you should have used counter-battery fire. And where were the professional artillery officers in your organisation to give you that advice? Or if they gave you that advice, did you choose to ignore it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: This is fascinating, but I don't think we can go further into this. The failures of fire plans may be legion, but I think we now have to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I was hoping to learn something from my Sarajevo experiences about the actual conduct of battle-field fighting, but that was not to be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, it might have been to your advantage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Major. I hope that this experience is going to suffer the fate like any other experience; it comes when it's too late. I hope that I will never have to face another war in my lifetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you do agree that we have professional artillerymen manning our artillery pieces; right? We had professional artillerymen, professional gunners, and so on, also fire observers, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree, and that's why I don't understand the random firing into the residential areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm asked if we can just slow down a little, because the French translation that Judge Lattanzi is depending upon is much slower than the English translation. That's not a criticism; it's just the question of linguistics. So if the parties could slow down a little. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further on, Major, in the Galic case, on the 30th of May, 2002, on page 9275, you said: [In English] "It's impossible to determine who fired the mortar shell that landed in the market square." [Interpretation] It pertains to Markale I on the 5th of February, 1994. It was not a verbatim quote, but this is the core of the matter. Is it true that it couldn't be established, where the shell had come from?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That is correct. In my view, it was inconclusive. It could not be established, who fired that mortar round. And I have gone on record already as saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 9th of February, 1994 - 65 ter 11035, that's the English version - in relation to that your answer was: [In English] "... answer this specifically. In the case of the Bosnians, the only sniper position I visited was under control of the minister of the interior. I could not get authority to visit the Bosnian sniper positions going through military authorities." [Interpretation] Further on, Judge El-Mahdi asked you: [In English] "On the Serb side, I had the feeling that it was controlled, at the brigade or even battalion level, that there would be instances of sniper fire which appeared to me to be done within a battalion area and had no references to the overall corps situation." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your statement of the 18th of November - 0055-2647 is the page reference - you said that sniper activity of the Bosnian side was hard to control, but on the Serb side that was true to a lesser degree. I mean, these difficulties were present on the Serb side to a lesser degree. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. And if you're talking about the apparent contradiction, it means that to get sniper fire stopped on the Bosnian side, I was going to have to go to the police, not even within my terms of reference and normal liaison, whereas on the Serb side, if there was sniper activity, I could go to the local brigade commander and get -- and actually get some action done. I hope you don't mind me anticipating his question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Not at all. An accurate anticipation is actually useful to both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, was that a bit unusual, that sniper activity of the Muslim side was under the police?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, and I have to say that I'm very biased. As a military commander, I don't like people shooting in my area that I don't control. So, of course I felt it was unusual, and I also didn't think that it was a good idea, but this was not my war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In a UN report here -- or, rather, an UNMO report of the 29th of June, 1995 -- you were no longer there by then, but the report is a significant one, and it says -- well, the document is 65 ter 09840, and could it please be called up in e-court. It says that observers saw that the parking-lot of the PTT building had been fired at, but it was not possible to establish who had fired that projectile. Do you agree that there were very many incidents and projectiles that remain un-dealt [as interpreted] with, their origins could not be established?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Before you answer, we're not getting that 09840 on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told it's a duplicate of 65 ter 09837.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps that can be put up.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously, we have the problem of two documents here. One pertains to a projectile. It is assumed that it's a modified aerial bomb. This is a report signed by Mr. Hansen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does the name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, and I can't comment on that because it's a projectile which I would have to see. It doesn't appear to be any normal projectile. And I can't comment any further on a document -- this document, because it doesn't appear to be an artillery piece. I might say, as an aside: As a general rule in Sarajevo during my time there, which ended in July 1994, that any mortar round could be fired by either side, but anything bigger than that generally had to have come from the Serb side. That was our first basic start point of any investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The document refers to the British Cymbeline building. Is that a reference to the Cymbeline tracking radar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I'm sure, Your Honour, there is a reference to the tracking radar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, sir, it is correct that at that point in time you were not there, but is this not a typical report of the UNMO Sector?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, it isn't. The fact that this particular incident was -- got merited a special report on its own, it was not included in the routine sitrep, means that, in fact, it was a special case, and because of there's so much description of the projectile. During my time in Sarajevo, the parking-lot was hit quite a few times by artillery fire, both mortar and artillery, and we did not create a report like this, because the projectiles were clearly identifiable as either mortar or higher weight of artillery. And I had a standing rule for all my military observers going to their vehicles to have their flak-jackets and helmets on the minute they left the door and the protection of the PTT building because of precisely that fact, we had so many impacts in the parking-lot. So for somebody to make this special report indicates that it was an extraordinary projectile and needed special treatment in the reporting system. But I can't comment on the contents whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in the case of special events, would then this be a usual report? If we have a special event, would this type of report then be the usual thing?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, in fact, the title says "Special Report."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can see it says here that it was established that it came from the Muslim side. Can we look at the following page, please.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Your Honour, since I didn't see the projectile and I have no idea, I cannot comment on a document where I have no idea what we're talking about, in terms of the physical round that I've been asked to comment on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That must be right. Dr. Karadzic, this is an illustration of the futility of putting documents to a witness that's either out of the time that they were in Sarajevo or, indeed, out of the normal range of activity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then should we wait for another occasion in order to be able to tender this and have it admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. It can be done through a Bar table motion or adduced through another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, sir, in the case against President Milosevic, on the 12th of November, 2003, on page 28883, as for uniforms, did you state that the blockade of Sarajevo prevented Muslims from obtaining uniforms from anywhere, and that they didn't have enough uniforms in the town, and that the result of that was that Muslims wore parts of uniforms? And you also confirmed that the Muslim side used sniper -- yes, well, this was about uniforms. And in the Galic case, on the 31st of May, 2002, page 9393 to 95, you said that the Muslim side used sniper fire in order to provoke a response from the other side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: You've asked me two questions. I'll answer them in the order that you've given them. The first one is, yes, the air-lift and the NATO -- the United Nations relief convoys did not bring in military uniforms. I'm sure you would have objected if they had. And, therefore, the Bosnian forces did not have enough uniforms. And as you know from your own background, any male that was of military age and either the Bosnian or the Serb side was supposed to be a soldier, whether, in fact, they wore the uniform or not. And, therefore, it's no surprise to find that we find people on the front-line, perhaps even without weapons, digging trenches, and they're not wearing uniform. And I think that happened on your side as well, only we weren't able to observe it as much because you didn't let us get close enough. On the case of the snipers, yes, I have been on record as saying that sniper fire was used to provoke retaliatory fire, which, of course, you responded in retaliation instead of in a military manner, waiting to see what was going to come of it, and you fired immediately and killed some people in no-man's land who were taking advantage of a temporary cease-fire that I had arranged. In fact, several of my own military observers were caught. We had arranged a cease-fire during the World Cup 1984 -- 1994, which, of course, I will remind the Court was won by Brazil, and the belligerents in that particular zone agreed to moderate their activities to permit all involved to watch the World Cup on TV, which as you'll recall was being televised from North America. And during the middle of the night, we found having a presence in the trenches had got people to stop shooting at each other. Well, that little cease-fire was broken up when a Serb football player on the battalion team was killed by a sniper. I maintain, and it's my personal view, that that was done at the instigation of somebody probably on the Bosnian political side who felt that the cease-fire wasn't good for the war. But that is one man getting killed, and immediately your battalion open fire on everybody and anything that moved on the other side. Unfortunately, three women were out in their back garden, taking advantage of the cease-fire trying to get some vegetables out of their garden, and three of my UNMOs went in to try and help them and they were shot at too. And I had to personally intervene with the battalion commander to get the firing stopped. So, yes, and I'll use a saying that prepared me well for tour in Yugoslavia: There are no good guys, only victims --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, sir, Major, if you pay attention to the Prosecution, you will see how Mr. Hayden is very satisfied with these assumptions of yours. But I would like you to answer precisely and not speculate. I would like you to answer my questions - my time is limited - because I find your answers are quite broad and are of assistance to the Prosecution, which is not in threat -- in danger here. I'm the one who is under attack here in this case. So, Major, sir, did you state, in your statement of the 13th of May, 2009, on page 10, the following? This is paragraph 47 of the statement: "The commanders of the Bosnian side --" [In English] "... much more conscious of their hierarchy and possibly also because of age and experience, they did not feel so confident in making agreements without consulting high authorities. In comparison, some Bosnian Serb brigade commanders, that is, at Igman and Vogosca, seemed to be confident in making local agreements"? [Interpretation] Was that so?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I made that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in that sense, was it easier for you than to reach some kind of agreement with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: With the battalion -- with the brigade commanders and the units under their command, for local agreements, yes, it was easier to make -- reach an agreement, such as the temporary cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now in the case against General Galic, on the 31st of May, 2002, on pages 9393 to 95, I will have to quote. The question was: [In English] "As regards to those civilian areas, Witness, the question is the following: As a tank officer, how can you formally and definitely exclude the presence of mobile military targets of any sort which would be located in a civilian zone, what one can consider to be a civilian zone when firing is ongoing?" [Interpretation] Your answer was: [In English] "The question is difficult to answer in just yes and no. It depends whether I am already on the ground or whether I am arriving after to determine my conclusions. Do you want me to proceed? "Q. No, I will refrain my question. Witness, you observed -- were observing fire in a zone that you considered to be a civilian area; is that correct?"

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. And the question was: "How, if you can -- how can you categorically rule out that at the moment of the firing, or perhaps a bit before the firing, there hadn't been, on that particular spot, a kind of military mobile object? "A. In some cases, I couldn't rule out; in some cases, I could." [Interpretation] Is that what you said in this case against --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, and I see no reason to change that statement I made at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean, Major, that you received information or were informed by the Muslim side that something was happening somewhere, or that you saw from a distance that something was happening, and then after a certain amount of time you were actually able to get there?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, it means that we saw artillery fire coming down on an area where a recent patrol indicated there was no military target of any value. And if -- bearing in mind the limited resources, if the Bosnian side had moved a military target to that area of significance, like a tank or a vehicle with soldiers on it, we would have been so surprised to see them actually having any mobile assets that we probably would have followed it to see where it was going, as we did with Serb vehicles when the exclusion zone was set up, we followed tanks, which you're very familiar with. And we would have done the same thing because we would have been so surprised to see mobile assets being used by the Bosnian Army. I'm sure it would have been reported from the minute they left the tunnel entrance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Major, can you assist with this: I think it's not disagreed that the Bosnian forces were in possession of mortars of various calibres, including up to 120 millimetres. In your direct observation, how were those being transported? Were they in jeeps or bigger vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think they were mainly being used -- manhandled. Of course, the most -- if I'm permitted to digress slightly and use up a little time, I'll tell you the most novel use of transport was a mortar that was put in an unused railway car near the PTT building, was pushed out by people on foot. It fired and then was pushed back before the Serb artillery reacted. So they were very innovative on how they moved the mortars, but I never saw them physically use a vehicle. And we spent a lot of time trying to catch them using -- moving mortars into the hospital grounds and then firing and then moving, but we were never able to pick them up doing it. But we know they did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just raise a point on the line of questioning that I think Mr. Karadzic -- Dr. Karadzic is pursuing, is that: It is true that we may have missed -- there were mortars being moved about in civilian housing, but the limited range -- for example, the 81-millimetre mortar can only shoot four kilometres, and if the 120-millimetre mortar is being used, moving it too far from the confrontation line means it can't be used. So we -- those artillery shells that fell into the center of the city out of range of the Bosnian artillery assets from reaching the front-line, they could not be engaging Bosnian artillery. And I still go back to my original statement I made earlier in this testimony, that the professional officers that Dr. Karadzic alludes to surely would have told them to use counter-battery fire. And as I've already stated in evidence submitted, I was, myself, under Bosnian mortar fire on the Pale road, and they were using a technique that I was quite impressed with, linear artillery barrage along Pale Road. And this is a unit that's improved its fire efficiency. If any unit should have been struck by counter-battery fire, this is the unit. It is using sophisticated mortar techniques. Instead, we were stopped on that road for over two hours, more than enough time to organise almost any kind of artillery response to deal with a vastly improved Bosnian mortar asset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Major. I think there's a danger perhaps of you attributing to the forces that you were dealing with, the expertise of the Canadian Armed Forces, but I didn't stop you because I thought Dr. Karadzic may have found your observations quite useful, from his point of view. It comes to this, then: that the Bosnian Army were or became capable of using mortars effectively; that the 81-millimetre mortar had a range of -- maximum range in the order of four kilometres, the 120 kilometre mortar you didn't give the maximum range, but that's at the longer range than four kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and unfortunately I don't have the range at the top of my head. It's not an equipment that we use. Our potential opponents in the 1990s, or the 1980s, rather, the Soviets, had a 120-millimetre mortar, and if I had a handbook here it would be easy -- but it was limited. As a standard rule, artillery guns vastly out-range mortars. Mortars, the projectile system, they get -- they're dropped down a tube, and the impact on the bottom of the round fires the missile, as opposed to ammunition that's loaded and you can adjust the charge to carry it even further. So a standard military piece -- the 105-round artillery used by the Bosnians, given to them by the Americans, would be in an aid package before the war. That could fire out beyond 14 kilometres, depending on the type of shell. The Russian artillery was famous for its long range. The 122-millimetre could fire out beyond 20 kilometres, and the 152 could also fire out, supposedly, depending on the ammunition type and how many bag charges, out to beyond 30 kilometres. So we're talking about a weapons system that there's a disparity in the use. Now, with super ammunition and the French model of 120-millimetre mortar, I do know that they had ammunition that could go out to 10 kilometres, but I don't know the figures for the Soviet-style equipment used by the Bosnian Serb or the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. And, again, I can't give any evidence, of course, but it might be agreed that one of the great advantages and tactics of mortar weapons is the shoot-and-scoot, where you fire and move so that your position cannot be struck by retaliatory fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is very true, as the Americans discovered in Vietnam. But that's one of the interesting things we watched very carefully in Sarajevo, and it still doesn't change the fact that the mortars that were firing -- I mean, the Serbs were able to discover mortars firing from beside Papa 2 and Papa 5 and retaliate with fire. I'm just a bit surprised that they couldn't just as quickly discover mortars firing on the Pale road and retaliate with fire then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it, but it seems to be your evidence that the Bosnian Army was certainly mortar capable, whatever the defects in the reaction from the Serbians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to speak more slowly for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. I would say, actually, I saw an improvement in the use of mortars during my time there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That took rather longer than I anticipated, Dr. Karadzic. That is time that will not be deducted from your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This is quite some help in clarifying matters. Can we look at the map. This is the moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, were you familiar with the entire area of Sarajevo? Did you know where Ilijas, Vogosca, Ilidza were, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I knew at the time in 1993 I could find my way around Sarajevo with no lights. Today, after having done a tour in Haiti and other places, I don't know whether I'll remember. I'll have to have a map to trigger, and I don't even know if I'll remember from the topographical features. But, yes, at the time I certainly knew my way around, but not as well as somebody like yourself who lived there --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Igman, so you knew the disposition of forces. Would you be kind enough to assist us? Can we now look at Map 32 now, 0546-6589 from the special binder. If you would just help us with the disposition of forces, and also the artillery and the weapons at the disposal of each of the two sides. This is Map 32. I don't know the 65 ter number, but the ERN number is 0546 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: It's in evidence as D311.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must ask you, Dr. Karadzic, while it comes up on my screen: What time-frame are we talking about? Are we talking about the time of General Mladic's attack across in August of 1993? Are we talking about the disputed time in December 1993, which was during my time? Are we talking about other attempts to block Mount Igman by both sides in the months that followed, or -- just give me a hint of what time you're talking about, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am convinced that you know that this was the disposition of forces or the line of separation throughout the entire war. As soon as you see this, you will see that that's what that is. I just wanted you to -- Major, do you see this map, and do you know what's what on this map? Would you agree that this is the inner part of town and that the broader area of the town was under the Serb control?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Until the map is clear to me and comes up a bit better, I can't really comment. And you also have it -- what date are we even talking about? There's no date of when these dispositions were made. For example, this map doesn't even seem to correctly place Hrasnica on the far side of the airport, and the salient that was created by General Mladic going towards the ski hill and the ski jump is not really shown on this map either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Just to point out for the Court there is, in fact, a date for this map on the bottom right-hand corner, the 31st of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Can it be enlarged slightly for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if it's 1995, I don't feel I can comment further, because as we know, NATO forces, they had that special brigade that was set up on top of Mount Igman, and I'm not sure when it came in, but it was -- I thought it was early -- it was a factor in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, if you don't feel that you -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: If you don't feel you're competent to comment, then, of course, you mustn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, sir, was the disposition of forces different, or was the map of the disposition of forces different when you were there than this one? I don't think so, other than this minor change in the north. Was this also the disposition of the forces at the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I do not -- I can't comment, because, first of all, I'm not satisfied with the portrayal of the Igman area. And the Igman area, without a doubt, was probably changed because there was NATO troops deployed on Mount Igman, if my understanding -- in 1995, but I don't know the exact dates. By then, I was in Haiti, so I think you'll have to get another witness to comment on this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, Major, I insist for you to say whether this is Igman and whether you had included the weapons at Igman as part of the Muslim contingent of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: If -- Your Honour, I can't comment on this map. There was a weapons collection programme, for which there are documents and reports, and that identified Mount Igman as one of the areas where there was a problem collecting weapons. But beyond that, I can't comment. I can't remember the details, and I can't -- this map is 1995, and I do know the situation at Mount Igman is not the way I feel it was in my time there in 1993/1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, there you have it, Dr. Karadzic. There's no point in pursuing this if the witness doesn't feel competent to give answers. And let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like some help to find a map that could -- that the major could give comments on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I'm trying to do, Major, is to establish whether there were Muslim forces and heavy weaponry around the Serbian forces as well. You were an observer, and we cannot just leave this uncovered.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can answer the question about heavy weapons. There may have been 120-millimetre mortars on the Bosnian positions on Mount Igman, although I don't think they were there during my time. But mortars, as you've corrected pointed out, can be concealed and moved. But most definitely one of the things we tracked about the Bosnians was their heavy weapons and where they moved, and if they -- when they took the tank out -- tanks out to fire, it was a special report incident. On the other hand, a tank from the Serb side firing was not a special report incident. It was included in the shell reps or the shelling reports of the day. And if there had been a tank or heavy artillery on Mount Igman, we would have seen it and it would have been reported. And bear in mind the French were also present on Mount Igman from the end of General Mladic's offensive action there in the summer of August 1993. There was a French contingent on top of Mount Igman, and they also would be very concerned about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at Map 25 from this binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a map from your time that includes the exclusion zones. I'm afraid, Major, that you are being partial, so I really have to change my line of questioning in order to eliminate this bias, with your goodwill, so that we can determine what's what, and you can just leave General Mladic alone. Do you agree, General -- sir, that we surrendered the area of Igman to you that we had liberated in the course of 1993? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, I feel that that area became a no-man's land, because the Bosnians would go forward at night and then during the day you'd kill them, and they -- if they were found forward. One of the battles I had during my time there was I felt that unarmed military observers weren't the people to be sitting there monitoring these violations. We asked the French to put a platoon on the best position there, and the French Battalion commander was over-stretched with his resources - at least that was the reason he gave - and they didn't feel that they could maintain a position at night on top of this feature that overlooked no-man's land, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, we'll take a break now and resume sitting again at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, were you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say a few words, if possible, Excellencies. I would like to ask, kindly, to be given more time. This is a very important witness. Over seven or eight or nine months, very important things happened, it was practically a turning point in our war, and that's when he was there. He's a participant in all these events. Unfortunately, he tends to speak at length. He also is not concealing his dislike of General Mladic. So I would kindly ask that I be given some more time tomorrow, because in spite of this high degree of partiality, we are going to get to some truths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: No, Dr. Karadzic, quite apart from the observation that you may be being very unfair to the witness, you're not here, nor are we here, to deal with General Mladic. But your observation about times when that's already been taken on board, and we are currently exploring the possibilities of extending the sitting time allowed -- cross-examination time allowed, but how the mechanics of that is going to work is still the subject of discussion and has to be taken into account that neither the witness nor I are available tomorrow afternoon. So we're dealing with it as best we can. In the meantime, please be as expeditious as possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm sure that that will depend on both sides. Can I ask for 65 ter 13636 in e-court. It's a map, 13636.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, in the meantime, let me ask you whether you took part in establishing and controlling the exclusion zone of 20 kilometres in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this the map of the exclusion zone? We're going to see it right now. Can we zoom in a bit, please. Is that the map of the exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It resembles the map. I can't be -- confirm definitely for legal reasons, because I haven't got a protractor to measure exactly, and there was a dispute about where, in fact, the centre of the exclusion zone was, which, to the best of my knowledge, never resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you remember, have a look at the north-west, Cekrcici. An area there was not included if the zone is in Marin Dvor, by the church. It's that map, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, that is -- there is -- there was a dispute about the exclusion zone. This is a map that I didn't use, so I can't be -- I can't make definitive statements about it. I can say that it appears to be a 20-kilometre exclusion zone, but I can't even read the scale on the map that I have adequately to say that even. If it could be blown up a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that they wrote "no screen available," so we cannot establish that. However, Major, do you agree that later on the PTT building was declared the center of the zone? In that case, Cekrcici was included. While the center was in Marin Dvor, Cekrcici was outside the exclusion zone; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That happened after my time and I'm not party to the resolution of that debate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we go back to the way the map looked before so that we can mark certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's start from the south, Major. Do you see the difference between the blue and the red lines? There's a small zone there. That is the south-west. Is that the zone that we abandoned and handed over to the UN?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That was -- happened after my time. I'm not going to make a statement one way or the other, if you're talking about the hand-over in 1995. Now, are you talking about what became no-man's land in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1993. It's not no-man's land. We'll see tomorrow, from General Briquemont's documentation, that this was handed over to the UN. But at your time, don't you remember that the Muslim side went through this zone, unauthorised, and they killed 20 of our military medical staff, some nurses? Do you remember that incident?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll get back to that. Tell me, is that Igman, the blue part there? Is that under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: On this map, but this map has the exclusion zone on and it's dated a different date. So it actually says two -- I can't pick out the actual date, so I have no way of knowing who drew that blue area and -- but -- so I can't comment on a map that isn't -- that I'm not familiar with. There was an area that the UN may or may not have assumed -- and there was a Mount Igman agreement, and if this had been a point of discussion for me to answer, I even have retained personal documents dealing with the Mount Igman agreement. But I can tell you, in December 1993 the issue was Muslim -- the Bosnian forces moving forward into an area which was under dispute and at night, and the issue for me was whether I was going to maintain the presence -- the UN presence on the hill that dominated that feature or whether the French would. And it was felt the French could deter it. But in any case, this was never designated, in our opinion, as UN-controlled area. It certainly wasn't for my military observers. We travelled through that area as if it was no-man's land, because there were Serb positions that could fire into that area and there were often Bosnian positions that could fire in that area, and none of us wanted to be there when both sides started firing at the same time or even one side or the other. And you're continuing to press me on this map, which I don't feel comfortable dealing with. It's costing us both more time. Sorry, Your Honour, to get -- add enlightenment to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, this position was there from the beginning until the end of the war. Are you saying that here in Igman, in this area where the little flag is that is under Muslim control, you're saying that there weren't any Howitzers there of 155, 122 millimetres, and other heavy weaponry? Was there such weaponry there or not? Any answer will do. Just tell us.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, there was no weapons there during my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Operations Group Pazaric to the left here, "Pazaric," that's what it says in Cyrillic, was there any heavy weaponry there?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: We were never -- got access into that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: It's going to be very difficult to understand the transcript, with references like "to the left of a flag." There is a number of flags on here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Karadzic, I don't know exactly what area you're referring to either.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] West of Igman, west of Igman, and it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: "West of Igman" covers a rather large area on the map. It is anywhere west of Igman. You'll need to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here "OG Pazarici," unfortunately, in Cyrillic. That is Operations Group Pazaric. Can we see the map on a smaller scale again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, do you agree that around the Serb forces there were Muslim and Croat forces? On this map and generally speaking, in real life, around these Serb forces, to the west, south and north, there was the Muslim Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll answer this question with a little detail. We were never allowed access through the Serb areas to gain into that area to patrol. The only surveillance of that area, and it was outside or was on an area between us and the Malaysian Battalion which occupied the sector to the east -- to the west, that area was too difficult for us to access, and the only surveillance was provided by French helicopters after the cease-fire, when they were no longer being fired at by belligerents of both sides. So I would suggest that I cannot answer Dr. Karadzic's -- and he knows very well why we didn't have patrols there. And I'm not being antagonist. I just feel that he must have been aware of the standard Serb policy of restricting our access to certain areas, and therefore this is an area he would know full well that we did not have very much access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, even today you are being hostile to the Serb side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, don't make statements. The Court will determine whether there is any hostility and what the effect of it is. Just use your remaining time more precisely. It's perfectly plain that the witness doesn't feel comfortable dealing with this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My last question in relation to this map, and then we're going to remove it. Could you have known that shells were falling on the Serb part of Sarajevo precisely from this area? Did you know that they were falling, and did you know where they were coming from, and did you express any interest in this area that was under the control of the Muslim and Croatian Army, and Serb territory was semi-encircled by these forces? If shots are falling on Ilidza, Ilijas, Vogosca, Lukavica, these shells were not fired from the inner-city, but from further beyond. Did you have any interest in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Objection. Your Honour, that's at least four questions in there. It should be broken out. The witness can't be expected to answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It must be right. There's a compound question, Dr. Karadzic, in other words, a number of questions contained in one continuous flow. But we've got the transcript. Taken question by question, are you able to answer it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can answer the first question about were we interested. Yes, we were interested whenever shells fell. First of all, I don't remember the brigade commander in Ilidza drawing my attention to brigade -- shells falling. Secondly, as the previous eye-witness statement and all of the testimony that I've given in the three cases indicate that I had so many OPs in the Sarajevo area, and to repeat ad nauseam the statement, I had my OPs that were on the Serb side were oriented to the fire units to count the shells being fired at Sarajevo, and the units based in the city were counting the shells that fell in the city. We did have not -- we did patrols, but we had limited resources to go to that area, even if we had got -- received a report. We do know that shells fell on the city from Croatian artillery, and that was identified and reported separately. Now, I'm surprised to hear from Dr. Karadzic that the Croatians fired on Ilidza, when we, in the year 1993, identified Croatian shells falling in Sarajevo proper. And that isn't in any of the documentation because it's not part of this investigation. But now that Dr. Karadzic raised Croatian involvement, I feel justified in bringing that point in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: What was the frequency of Croatian shelling during your period in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only reason -- not very often. The only reason I remember this distinctly is that when I was trying to explain to people about the convoluted nature of the war in Yugoslavia, I used the example of the Croatians in Kiseljak firing on the Croatians in Sarajevo, because some of the shells fired from Kiseljak which were tracked fell in the city that was being held by Croatian units of the Bosnian forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, how far away is Kiseljak from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you agree that it says here "HVO Kresimir"? That is in the middle of this map, but further to the west. That's what it says on this map. So the Croatian Army was there, and they could have targeted Sarajevo even from there.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: The Croatian Army shelling that we traced -- tracked came from the area of Kiseljak. That is my response.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Major, when you spoke about the number of heavy weapons that the 1st Muslim Corps had, you meant the weapons that was in the very center of the city, the territory that they held, the inner-city; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I spoke of the weapons that were within the besieged city that you were surrounding over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for every one of these observations. If you were to add to those weapons the weapons that were outside this ring of Muslim-Croat forces, would that change the ratio involved and would that make the weaponry ratio work in favour of the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I have no idea how many weapons we're talking about. The weapons within the exclusion zone were supposed to be accounted for, and I left Sarajevo while there was still a dispute about the weapons and what should be held on Mount Igman. I'm sure that there is documentation available to you and to the Court that subsequently deals with the Mount Igman weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, between Vogosca and Sarajevo there was a Lima position, wasn't there, and also near Ilijas to the south-west? Did you have an OP there?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, not an OP, per se. We had -- initially, as I said, before the cease-fire we had positions which -- that were primarily there to record when your fire units shot into Sarajevo. As a secondary mission, as all military observers do, they reported on what they saw as well. This was a standing secondary task of every single military observer in Yugoslavia. He reported on what he saw subsidiary to his -- whatever his primary task was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That goes without saying. Major, my last question in relation to this map: From where were shells falling on Ilijas, in the corner of the exclusion zone up here? Where were shells fired from, those that fell on this Serb municipality?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, weren't your observers supposed to know that it was falling -- that they were falling from Visoko? That is contained in your reports, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No. The -- Visoko was being -- that area was actually being done by CanBat II, a Canadian unit, and the boundary ended short of Visoko. So if there was Bosnian fire units engaging units in Sector Sarajevo from outside our boundary, we would not follow up and investigate. And we had enough to do with the tasks we had monitoring your units firing into Sarajevo and reporting the shells falling, and we did not have resources, except to send a patrol out to investigate all too often after the fact. And if there had been more raised about this issue, we could have considered setting up an OP there, like we did after the cease-fire, but we did not receive full co-operation and, in fact, the OP that was finally set up in that area was set up by the Canadian Reconnaissance Unit as part of the Canadian Battalion and not by UNMOs. And I was, remember, negotiating in June, trying to get an OP set up in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Major. We're going to conclude that particular topic. Would it help you, to avoid that discrepancy between incoming and outgoing fire, if you took into consideration that Serb-held territory could be fired at from outside Sarajevo, from Central Bosnia? Wouldn't it have been clearer then, who had what and who was firing with what?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It may be correct, but my responsibility was for Sector Sarajevo and not for those areas outside. There was another senior military observer who had units of his organisation in Visoko and also in the Malaysian Battalion area, and I think you also are aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I thought that you were a single army, not national units, Major. Thank you, we can remove this map. We won't be signing it, because the major cannot recognise a map from his own time. Major, is it correct that you were victims of incidents in Sarajevo -- or, rather, that you identified victims of incidents in Sarajevo in morgues or in medical institutions?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How could you make a distinction between a victim who was killed at a scene -- at a site that was reported to you as the scene of an incident from another body that was brought in from the front-line?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Generally, by shrapnel and because, if possible, we tracked the bodies from the incident, through the collection point at the district, and down to the morgue. So, of course -- in the case of the one that I personally tracked, the young lady of 19 was killed by a 20-millimetre round in her apartment, on the telephone. I saw her later, when I was with another patrol, at the central -- her body at the central collection point, and I saw her that night when I went on the patrol that goes to the morgue. So as you notice from the casualty lists that we have documented, we just identify the total number of casualties. We didn't try and separate, on the report that went to Zagreb, whether they were on the front-line, or on the way to the front-line, or from the front-line. We didn't have the resources to make all those distinctions that you would like to have now in this court. So if you look at the totals, Your Honour, you will see that we just listed dead, and you have to assume the soldiers we hope were killed on the front-line, though if they had made good use of artillery, some of them may have been caught out behind the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who examined the bodies from the outside, and in what way? Actually, on your side, who carried out the external examination of the body and established the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: We used ordinary military observers, like myself, and we went in. And if the body -- and I must say I've never heard a report of somebody dying from a non-bullet wound in that period, but the bodies were clearly identifiable by missing limbs, pieces of shrapnel, that they were the victims of either shelling or, in some rare cases, bullet fire. In other words, there would be a bullet hole in their head or in some part of their body. So it doesn't take a very difficult thing, and I've seen bodies in the course of my seven UN missions, to find out that I don't need to be a doctor to identify the cause of death as violent action in conflict with a heavy round, or a light round, or some kind of bullet. Also, the presence of a lot of blood gives you a clue as well; dried blood, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're trying to say, Major, sir, that the external examination of a body, as a forensic act, was not carried out by a forensic expert. You didn't strip the bodies; you just conducted an external examination and provided that kind of description of the body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. Some nights, there were 600 bodies. We did not have any trained forensics, and I doubt if they would have gotten through all the bodies that were in the morgue in time. And we were very careful to identify to make sure we were not identifying a body twice, and that is the main concern we had, because most of the bodies, and I'm only speaking for the one night that I accompanied one of my patrols, but they carry this procedure out every night, it was not a favourite task and it certainly entailed looking at people that they could clearly identify had been subjected to some kind of violent activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The lines of separation or the front-lines, were they shelled by each of the sides?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Someone who is killed at the line of separation by a shell, what category would you put them in; as somebody who was killed on the front-line or somebody who was killed in firing in the town? How could you tell these two apart?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I was -- already dealt with that earlier in a question from the Prosecution. Males were assumed to be soldiers, females were assumed to be civilians, and the military observer had to use his judgement in the context. And some of these people, no doubt we mis-identified them as civilians. And some of the people -- and I go back to the girl that I tracked. She, in fact, was a courier for the military, but we classed her as a civilian because she was killed in the course of trying to phone her boyfriend, not in the trench where she normally worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same way, did you register the casualties on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: We tried to. I've tried to several times organise, through the liaison officer at Lukavica, a visit to the Serb hospitals. Ideally, we would have liked to have had the same arrangement on the Serb side as we had in Sarajevo. We would visit hospitals on a routine basis every day, and also visit the morgue or morgues on a routine basis every day. When General Galic finally allowed himself to see me, it was too late to start this process, because by then I was over-tasked trying to make sure NATO didn't bomb his guns because they were not moving fast enough to the parts where they were supposed to be stored. But certainly from the time I arrived in July -- correction, October, I tried to have the same arrangement made with the Serbs as I had with the people inside. And you will note consistently throughout my sitreps, if you've bothered to read them all, that I consistently said that we did not have enough observation on the Serb side for the casualties they were taking. And I feel strongly about the civilian casualties that you did not allow me to see, because perhaps we could have done something to prevent their relatives from getting killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're speaking of Serb civilian casualties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. I'm speaking of those Serb casualties that you did not tell me about, that you did not allow me to see in the hospitals, and that you did not allow me to count in the morgues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That surprises me, Major, sir, because in documents here we have the fact that out of 80, you had 11 observation posts, Lima on the Serbian side and 3to 5 Papa observation posts on the Muslim side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, and I have to repeat again that the positions of the observation posts on the Serb side were primarily set up, at least until after the cease-fire, to observe your units firing. What better way to count what ammunition is being expended than to actually watch the rounds loaded? And they were not in a position to observe the inhabited areas, which were much greatly spread out in the surrounding Serb area, and we had to get permission to visit the hospital. And consistently, with few exceptions, this was denied. The casualties on the Serb side were obtained from your liaison officer or from personal observation on patrols. And we know that we tried to get this instituted. And, in fact, if you carefully read the sitreps, you'll see that that is one of the complaints that we consistently raised with Zagreb as well. I felt from the very beginning of my time there that the civilian casualties on the Serb side were not being adequately covered, and I felt that -- actually, that the Serb authorities, of which you count as the most senior, were placing obstructions in my path from finding out what these casualties were. And you were certainly not allowing me even to do the body counts, which the Bosnians were. Your Honour, time -- this is counting in his time, because I would be interested in the time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's counting in all our time. But, yes, of course, if you are able to answer a question simply yes or no, then please don't be constrained from doing so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D1868 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, sir, I cannot but say it. I see that you have the same sentiments towards General Galic. I would like to show his actual position, based on documents. And, Major, two generals, colleagues of mine, were sentenced to quite serious sentences here because they did not manage to throw light on the truth, so we are trying to do that. Now, we are looking at the order by General Galic about the cessation of hostilities, dated the 16th of June, 1993. And it states here: "Respect the mentioned cease-fire.
