Take the measurements to prevent ostensibly and responsible behaviour by some officers in the eventual disregarding of the agreement, especially regarding cease-fire. Immediately phone the superior officer SRK command and nearest UNPROFOR institution and others. Fire -- the commands of the brigades will offer every assistance to UNPROFOR in performing these tasks." And then the next page: "Ensure freedom of movement to UNPROFOR forces. Keep reporting ...," and so on and so forth. Major, sir, you had more observers on the Serbian side, but you were observing what Serbs were firing and not what was fired at them, and that is why we have this discrepancy here in the outgoing and the incoming projectiles that is so broad that they are not useful. They cannot be used in the legal and judicial context. Are you aware that General Galic had this position? And you can see from all of his documents that he had full respect both for the cease-fires and for UNPROFOR. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Not by his actions, I was not aware of that. If he was so open, why did he not come and let me meet him and discuss this order with him, and then give me access to the hospitals and to the morgues, as we wanted, instead of letting his liaison officer keep putting obstacles for me to actually even see him with this kind of request? And also why did people persist on shelling if this was -- it always comes back to the word "retaliation." Retaliation isn't a military operation. Actions speak louder than words, to use an old English phrase, and 1600 rounds fired in one day, which is half the ammunition allocated to the Canadian Artillery Battalion we had in Germany in 1985, is not the action of somebody following the instructions here signed by his -- not by General Galic, I notice, but by his chief -- his DM and MG.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, sir, we should ask your superiors about the restrictions put up by General Galic, because it's not customary for a major to reach a general at any time. Not even Major Indjic was able to reach the general on the other side at any time, and this is evident. We can hear this clear bias on your side. You cannot have access to General Galic whenever you wish, but the others of equal rank did. So I would kindly ask you to stick to your questions -- to your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: You're engaging in argument, and it's completely useless. It doesn't amount to evidence, it doesn't assist the Court, and it's wasting what remains of your time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this? Excellency, this depends on the witness. He is broadening the topics consistently, and he's showing hatred towards my generals. A major cannot have access to a general. A general can have access to a major. He cannot be slinging mud at him here like that after he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... for cross-examination if you don't apply your mind to doing it properly. I'm not going to give you unlimited time to engage in argument invective. It's quite simple. It's in your hands as to whether you get any further time or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document, please, so that I can call up the next document?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So be it. That will be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D629, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D1873 now. We are going to -- well, I'm going to refrain from comments, but we're going to substantiate everything with documents. And I'm kindly asking the major to stick to brief answers. 1D1873.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document that General Galic did sign, and I would just like to read this warning. I'm going to draw your attention to that. I'm going to interpret it briefly or read it: "All military conscripts are being warned that the behaviour towards the representatives of the international organisation UNPROFOR, UNHCR, MCK, UNICEF, and other structures of the UN, must be correct, avoiding also the least rudeness. The contact with them must be civilised, extremely cultured and polite, without raised voices, showing goodwill and readiness to provide them with complete security in their work." And so on and so forth: "It is essential to prevent the mistreatment and abuse of civilian Serb citizens that are employed in that force." This is a secret document, not intended for any kind of propaganda. It's a very strict command to subordinates to respect you, take proper action towards you, to see you; is that correct or not? And then it also says that no rough treatment should be permitted, improper comments -- even the improper comments are banned, and that you should be allowed the complete freedom of movement on roads. Were you aware of this policy, as stated?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, and I don't think it meant anything, because the colonel commanding the Ukrainian contingent was stopped for 24 hours at Rogatica in December 1993, so surely the people there did not understand this. And he was a colonel and deserved to be treated better, if you're going to pull rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you also will recall that the unit was held by women, dissatisfied women, whose husbands were captured in Gorazde; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No. You are completely -- got a different -- this is going to see his Ukrainian company in Zepa. It belonged to his contingent. He is the battalion commander as well as had a senior staff appointment as deputy commander of UNPROFOR in Sector Sarajevo, and he was made to wait for 24 hours. So where is this courtesy due to the proper rank? And by the way, I held a position which was filled by lieutenant-colonels before and after me. But maybe in the Canadian Army I can do the job of a lieutenant-colonel or maybe even a general in the Serb army, if you're going to throw insults. But, anyway, I'd like to hear your response to my question back to you. Why was the Ukrainian colonel detained for 24 hours in December?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Tempting though it may be, as a witness, I'm afraid you can't ask questions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: -- of the defendant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm going to satisfy your curiosity. We will come to that by way of documents. Can we put this document away, and can we look at another one which was issued a day after you arrived in Sarajevo? Can this document be admitted, this previous document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D630.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P830. We don't have to admit it; we just want to refresh the major's recollection. It's a document of the 16th of October, 1993, this is the following day after his arrival in Sarajevo. P830.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, so would you agree that this is of the 16th of October, and this is Victor Andreev informing Cedric Thornberry, and the drafter was David Harland, and then the last bullet point on the first page says: "The influence of organised crime appears to have reached unprecedented levels ..." [In English] "... especially in Sarajevo." [Interpretation] Did you know that the crime rate in Sarajevo had reached unprecedented levels?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I was aware of this memo. I was -- my second day in Sarajevo, I had no reason to believe it or disbelieve it. I didn't know the officer involved to prepare this memo, and I certainly don't believe paperwork that is handed in front of me, as you can recognise from my experience working with your forces who had a direct order not to harass us, obviously, paperwork can mean something or it can't, and it has to be verified. And I have lots of things to do when I'm taking over 200 military observers. I looked at this, and I was going to make my own judgement on that. I'm aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that we need to be cautious in relation to official reports by Victor Andreev, the civilian head -- the Civil Affairs head, to Cedric Thornberry, director of Civil Affairs? Do we need to demonstrate the caution that you have just spoken about vis-a-vis official documents of the United Nations? Should this be accepted as a reliable document or should we have some doubts in relation to this, which is what you have just said?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I read this document and I recognise this document. I decided I would make my own determination. I have no idea what the crime rate was in Sarajevo, for example, during the 1984 Olympics or the collaboration between the criminals and the -- on both sides of the belligerent lines. However, you should be aware that I did visit the chief of police in Sector Sarajevo as part of my taking command of the UNMOs there, and -- but I'm not going to disclose what we talked about, because obviously you had access to UN documents so you feel yourself very well informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the next page, please. The next page, the subheading is "The rump B and H." "In Sarajevo, the ethnic Muslim radicals appeared to be ..." [In English] " ... gaining the upper hand at the expense of moderates who favour a multinational BH society. BH-controlled Sarajevo is approximately 80 per cent ethnic Muslim. The non-Muslims are being replaced in government by Muslims, and non-Muslims are increasingly uncomfortable." [Interpretation] The following paragraph says: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... to the problem. Each personnel and facility is being used as conduits for black market goods. Civil Affairs personnel have also been touched (the local mafia had evicted Daljeet Bagga from his apartment at five minutes' notice; threatening calls have been made to Civil Affairs by black marketeers wanting press cards)." [Interpretation] And this one here, the food situation continues to be confusing: [In English] "... convoy deliveries have increased recently, but distribution by the BH government to Sarajevo citizen is still very limited. Large quantity. This food is directed to the military, and a smaller amount refers to the black market. The bulk of the missing aid, perhaps 60 per cent, remain unaccounted for. Speculation is that the BH government is stockpiling it." [Interpretation] Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I was aware of criminal activities, but my main function was to count the shells you fired into Sarajevo, which by my background as a common-arms officer, I'm familiar with in service of other UN missions where people shelled each other, and I was also interested in the capabilities of the Bosnian Army and the casualties that your shelling caused. The investigation of criminal activity in the civil society quite properly belonged to some other organisation. Perhaps the military investigates everything on the Serb side - I won't go into that area - but I think this is outside my purview to discuss what the Civil Affairs agency did with this allegation of criminal activities in Bosnia. And perhaps you're lucky that you didn't have this individual sitting in your side of the line finding out criminal activities in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, sir, so you are speaking the least about the most important parts. You have spoken 95 per cent of the time about things that have nothing to do with the number of shells, which was your main task, so you are actually broadening the subject-matter. You're speaking about things that are not -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: You can't ask questions relating to documents like this, which have nothing to do with this witness's remit in Sarajevo, as it's described, and then expect any other sort of answer than the one he gave. It's just a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, the witness is talking about things that have to do with matters in the document. He speaks about our conduct. He's judging the Serb side. He's speaking the least about what he says his main task was, the number or the counting of shells. We didn't hear much about that, and what we did hear is unreliable, other than the number of incoming and outgoing shells. So this witness is biased and has a hostile attitude towards our side. I mean, I accept the trial to protect my rights, and you did protect me on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I'll give you one last opportunity to absorb this. The question of hostility from a witness is one for the Court to judge and, if necessary, take action upon when coming to judgement on issues which are relevant to the indictment. Engaging in argument or insults or invective on either side is of no use to anybody and it simply wastes time. Moreover, the Court is not going to allow extra time for similar invective or engagement. I've said it before, this is entirely in your hands now as to whether or not you get any time beyond the time that the Court was going to sit for today. So if you can ask focused questions about those matters which you want answers from the witness, according to his expertise, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Excellency, I'm going to explain this. We're just looking for one document. Can we look at 14290. And the position of the Defence is as follows: We have a witness here who has a hostile attitude. He's very detailed and speaks about everything else, except for what he considers to have been his main task, which puts the Defence in a difficult position of dealing with matters that the witness just happens to mention in passing. It's not -- that is not the problem of the Defence. The problem is that many things are recorded in the transcript that then we need to deal with. We need to clarify them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Arguments -- trying to be argumentative with me is going to be very unproductive for you, indeed. If you simply get on with your job of cross-examination, then you may find that if it's going well, the Court will allow you extra time. If not, then you can readily see what the consequence will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, on the 11th of January -- or, actually, you were there until mid-1994. Do you see this document on the screen? Is it from your time?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a daily sitrep for Sector Sarajevo. I would like to draw your attention to the last part of section A -- 2(a), that is "Warring Parties Conflict Activity." And then it says here: [In English] "Bosnian forces were firing mortars from residential areas, and some of these positions were obviously targeted by BSA." [Interpretation] Is that what you had said, that the Serbs inappropriately or unskillfully responded to fire that was being opened against them from residential areas?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: In this particular case, as has already been pointed out by His Honour, the Bosnian forces cleverly used residential areas. Yes, they had a limited number of mortars and they did fire from residential areas, but not over the area that was hit by 1600 rounds or 3.000 on December 22nd. And it would be interesting to know whether you, in fact, fired back in these areas the day that followed. So if you call up the next sitrep, you could see that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page, please. I'm not going to be baited in this way anymore, and I'm not going to go into a debate, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you think it is permissible to place one's artillery and mortars in a residential area and to mask your military positions using civilian population?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, as I've made clear in my statement, which was presented by the Prosecution this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you believe that a mortar is artillery? Or, rather, which mortars are artillery and which aren't?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: A mortar is a mortar. An artillery can be divided into Howitzers and guns. That is my opinion. I don't care what category you use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I draw your attention and the attention of all participants to paragraph 9: [In English] "Other important incidents/patrols and investigations: "Bosnian school in West Sarajevo was hit by seven rounds, shells of 120-millimetre mortars, at 1030 hours this morning. One killed and four wounded. Confirmed by UNMOs. It appears that the rounds came from the south-west. It seems very likely that the rounds came from BSA weapons. However, the evidence is not conclusive. When questioned, Serb liaison officer strongly denied Serb responsibility." [Interpretation] Do you agree that Stup was under Croat control, not Serb control?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is an example of a misunderstanding, where it is believed that the Serbs had fired. In another place, you said that the Serbs had followed from Stup. Do you agree that Stup was under Croatian control, not Serbian?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No. It was -- Stup was a disputed area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at paragraph 14 here: [In English] "The use of riot control agents may represent an escalation in retaliation. The targeting of the school also represents a signal or is intended to mislead, depending on who fired. It is considered that today is only the beginning and that levels of military activities by both warring factions will now increase." [Interpretation] Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I agree with that assessment because I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D631, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D428.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, you said that for the most part, there was no artillery in town, that the Muslims did not have artillery in town, but you did say that there was artillery and mortars and tanks. However, allegedly or in your opinion, they were not used sufficiently. Now we're going to call up a document of the Muslim Army, the Supreme Command Staff. The 17th of October, 1993, is the date, so that's when you were there. 1D428. So that is the first page. Can we have a look at the third page, yes, towards the bottom. I'm going to read it, and probably there is no translation for the time being. The Intelligence Service of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina is writing this, and I'm just going to read the lower part: "On the basis of the information received from the State Security Service, we have learned that the former deputy commander of the staff of the UNMOs on the Papa side ...," now the next page, please: "... Russian Army Major Veselov Andrej, after serving in Croatia, was returned to Sarajevo again, and appointed to the head of observers on the Lima side," there's a typo here, "at Mrkovici." "As former deputy commander of the UNMO staff on the Papa side, Veselov is familiar with artillery positions and the types of artillery weapons that the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina has." So there is an anxiety here that this observer of yours, who was on the Serb side first and was then coming to their side, knew what the artillery positions on their side were in town; is that right, Major?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, this military observer was not there when I was there, so he had left before October of 1993, and the 14th of October, so I can't comment further. My predecessor probably dealt with this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, on the 17th of October, he returned, and he was transferred to the Lima side, the village of Mrkovici. For a while, he was on the Muslim side, and then in Croatia, and then the Serb side. So did the Muslim Army have artillery in town, itself?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: This report is dealing with an officer that I don't recognise, and I'd have to confirm, from the nominal role that I have in Canada, that he, in fact, even was serving. And I don't read any of the material that's on this report. I can't comment further. Unless it's translated, I won't comment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I did properly translate these paragraphs. I was checked by the interpreters. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We object to the admission of this document. The witness hasn't commented on any passage. As a side issue, it hasn't been translated. But we would not want it to be MFI'd, merely subject to translation. We object to its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, this witness really didn't assist with the admission of this document, and for reasons that he plainly stated. But it seems that they may be material in it which is useful and relevant, and what I suggest is that it's the subject of a Bar table admission, unless there is another witness that you can put it through, having been translated. I'm not going to mark it for identification, but if you wish to have a translation done of the parts which you think are relevant, then in due course it can come before us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have 1D1870.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that: Major, this is the Command of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's a report dated the 8th of December, 1993. Do we agree that in Sarajevo there was this 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina facing the Sarajevo Romanija Corps on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Several times, you noted that the Muslim Army far outnumbered the Serb Army, in terms of troops; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I said that the Bosnian Army had the advantage in manpower as an asset.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a report. It is actually a supplement to an order, strictly confidential, et cetera, the 1st Corps. And number 1 "The Aggressor," that's a paragraph that explains what the Serbs, the alleged aggressor, are doing. And then we're going to look at the last subparagraph of the first paragraph: "The battalion is mostly manned by locals and refugees from the Zenica area, and has not reached full complement. In previous combats, it suffered serious casualties." This is a reference to the Serb battalion. And then in paragraph 2, it says: "The Sarajevo Corps is carrying out a decisive defence on the lines reached and is carrying out attacks in the area of responsibility of the 5th Motorised Brigade and the 102nd Motorised Brigade, tasked with a simultaneous attack to break enemy forces on the following directions: Dobrinja-Nedzarici and Stupska Petlja-Nedzarici, and gain the area of Nedzarici as soon as possible." And then in paragraph 3, it says what the 101st Motorised Brigade is doing through activities carried out in concert -- they actually say towards the end of this paragraph that they will act in concert with their artillery forces. So let us start with "I have decided" now. We don't have to move on to the next page in English, but we do in Serbian: "I have decided: "Carry out actions from reached lines or chosen directions with concentration of strong artillery fire in preparation and in support. With simultaneous and synchronised strike inside the units with different forms of combat actions, with committing reconnaissance/sabotage groups, relying on suitable buildings on the ground, break and neutralise the enemy on p/k, and creating panic among Chetniks and civilians. Cary out attacks," et cetera, et cetera. Does this coincide with what you said attacks on Grbavica, Nedzarici are well-co-ordinated, planed, and carried out?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It would indicate they have a planning capability and this order was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that they are relying on strong artillery fire here and that they planned to cause panic among Chetniks and civilians?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I think that perhaps, as you might agree, the commander is making an assumption about creating panic. I think the word "artillery" is used probably to indicate mortar fire, which is indirect fire, mortars like artillery fire in an indirect fashion, and they were very good at using mortars. So I would say that the use of artillery in this order, and I have not seen the translation and I'm not sure what the actual translation would be, and I'm not considering that your translation is completely reliable - no offence to your Serbo-Croatian - but that the artillery that he's referring to could most likely be mortars, and that the attacks that he's talking about are well within the range of the 120-millimetre mortar. So -- and he -- as you have pointed out, yourself, he's very clever -- the Bosnians were very clever at moving the mortars up through residential areas, so that I'm sure they would be in range. So I think, golly, he must have -- he must have been trained at the Yugoslav Staff College. He wrote a very good order. And what was the Serb reaction? I mean, I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm not supposed to ask questions. I'm just curious, out of military curiosity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: I can understand that, but let's leave it at that. Mr. Hayden, you were -- no, it's been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I just remind you, Major, it says here in the decision: "I have decided to use artillery fire," to do this and that. He is ordering to create panic among civilians and Chetniks. "Strong artillery fire," that's what it says in the original and in the translation. During preparations and during the actual attack, the artillery is supposed to operate and create panic among Chetniks, that is to say, our soldiers, and civilians. Can we now have a look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I just comment on that? He's answered his own question, "supposed to create panic." Of course, the commander, what he writes on paper doesn't necessarily occur, and we know the Serbs didn't panic when they were being shelled in lots of cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: The real point may be, Dr. Karadzic, that you're asking the witness to go into the mind of another person, which is rarely productive. And if it's an accurate translation, the document seems to speak for itself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation is accurate. Anyone can check that. And it is true that it is in the section entitled "I have decided."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Right, Major? And he decides to carry that out; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: He agreed to -- he was going to attempt to use artillery fire to do what I think you were attempting to do with your artillery fire; create panic. And you, yourself, answered your question. "He supposed," you supposed that. And I would ask, Your Honour, if I can leave this. As you said, I am getting into the mindset of a corps commander, and as Dr. Karadzic pointed out, I'm only a major, so I wouldn't want to get into a general's premises.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we see paragraph 6. May I draw your attention to that? We have it in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Firing support." "Firing support of the 1st Corps in the area of Mount Igman. Watch tower in the area of Mojmilo. Open selective artillery fire in the most fortified buildings in the depth of enemy positions. Brigade artillery group of 5 and 102nd Motorised Brigade will open fire ...," et cetera, et cetera. So they are acting in concert with the artillery from town. Major, should UN Monitors know what the warring parties have; Not only the Serb side, that is, but the Muslim too?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, we tried our best, and it just validates my request to have patrols go into that area, patrols which you denied access to. It validates my concern about an area which we knew nothing about and which I had so much trouble getting into. Thank you for pointing that out. I'm glad to see that I was justified in wanting to get into that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will see from other reports, Major, that you actually didn't have access to the Muslims. But what prevented you from going to Igman and seeing what they were using to target the Serbs, and who hindered you from going to Sarajevo and seeing what their artillery pieces were?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: We did. We did know what their artillery pieces were in Sarajevo, as much as we could, and I'm sure we missed some, like the tank in the basement. No one ever thought they'd park a tank in a basement. But then we didn't get access to the area that you mentioned about on Mount Igman, and we tried. And if you were to look at the logs and present them as documents from your brigades in those areas, you would see the UN requested permission, if you kept logs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is what I'm putting to you, sir, on the basis of Muslim documents as well: that they had more than three tanks -- actually, at least three tanks, Howitzers, mortars, recoilless guns, mountain guns, and that there was artillery on Mount Igman and in town. We believe that you had to know about that. Now, we see that you didn't know that, that the UN didn't know that, and the Serbs could not prevent you from finding out about that. It really depended on the wishes of the Muslim leadership; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, I've already pointed out to you that we knew about the presence of artillery pieces in the city, but that they were being protected in the tunnel. And also we had a list of artillery pieces, but we didn't know where they all were, and we were trying to find out. And we were meeting obstacles in our attempts to find this out. And I have -- I must admit, Your Honour, if I can digress a minute, because I have a very strong bias about this particular area because of the fact that I had a patrol going into this area that was taken hostage by Mr. Karadzic's army, so I feel very strongly that I was not allowed access to that area. And I -- it -- that's -- I won't say anything further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, I can understand the pressures of giving evidence, especially about matters which are stressful, but the shorter the answer, generally, the better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, we could not have kept your people as hostages on Muslim territory. I asked you something different. Can this document be admitted? This document is of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and there is a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: No objection to its admission. I think as you alluded to, Your Honour, the witness wasn't able to speak to this, and in that respect it may have been more appropriate to have this submitted via a Bar table, through another witness. But we don't have an objection to its admission now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: That may have been the better route. But there's no point in doubling efforts, so we'll admit it now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D632, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D00346, could we have that, please. It is also an army bulletin, a bulletin of the Muslim Army, of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, dated the 24th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that: Major, let me ask you, did the UN army, at lower levels, I assume, did they trade with the Muslim Army, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Did they sell them oil and other resources? We saw about the jackets and helmets, but what about oil, fuel of the UN? Did it go to the Muslim Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this question -- first of all, let me make it clear that there was no evidence -- I mistook those people for French soldiers because of the equipment they are wearing, but there was no evidence, as I have stated twice already that they purchased that equipment from any UN sources. Secondly, the question he's asking me are more appropriately dealt with by battalion commanders of those respective nationalities who had troops in Sarajevo. As military observers, when I found somebody that was involved in trading with either side, I had them leave the area immediately, and my only regret is I didn't kick one guy out sooner. And if Mr. Karadzic doesn't know about him, obviously his intelligence failed, but I sent a man out for -- he was trading, and that's the only incident that I know of in my military observer organisation. And that's the only organisation I can speak for or will speak for, because I think the people in the national contingent should be given -- and probably somebody like General Rose would know all that detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: One moment, please, Dr. Karadzic. I just want to find out what the possibilities are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I just add to that, Your Honour, it's a question of black market activities by the other contingents. Anything I would say in this part would be hearsay and not admittable in any court in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, you may be surprised to learn that under certain circumstances, hearsay is admissible in this Tribunal, but I take your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It's almost half past 2.00, and, Dr. Karadzic, you would have had getting close to about three hours, about two hours and fifty-odd minutes. What we're doing is trying to find out, first of all, the realistic possibilities of continuing for a little while today, and, secondly, what the position is tomorrow. The difficulty with tomorrow is that one of the courtrooms, as you may know, is out of commission, which is a pity, but it constrains everybody. So what I'm proposing to do is to rise now for 15 minutes to give everybody a break. We will come back. If it's possible to continue for a while this afternoon, we will. If not, by that stage, hopefully, other arrangements might have been identified. But we'll find that out as soon as possible, and all parties will be informed. The reality is that nothing is going to happen, I can assure you, to interrupt with your travel plans.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. --- Break taken at 2.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of September, 2010.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.30 p.m.,
